title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
Checked 2026-11-16. Official docs fetched via a summarising fetch tool (quotes as returned). Nothing run against a model or cluster. Base: C = https://code.claude.com/docs/en/ ; O = https://opencode.ai/docs/ ; S = https://slurm.schedmd.com/ Decision fed: accuracy of quest text on HPC and notebook safety. “GENERAL PRACTICE” = not stated in any doc fetched; treat as advice, not fact.



CONFIRMED: sbatch “is used to submit a job script for later execution”; srun “to submit a job for execution or initiate job steps in real time”; squeue “reports the state of jobs or job steps”; scancel “to cancel a pending or running job or job step”; sinfo reports partitions and nodes. S quickstart.html (2026-11-16)
CONFIRMED: sbatch “exits immediately after the script is successfully transferred to the Slurm controller and assigned a Slurm job ID”. Default time limit “is the partition’s default time limit”. --test-only validates and estimates start, “No job is actually submitted”. --parsable prints only the job ID. S sbatch.html
CONFIRMED: “If necessary, srun will first create a resource allocation in which to run the parallel job.” So srun outside an allocation requests resources and (by default) runs synchronously. S srun.html (first 100k of 175k chars read; --pty entry not read)
CONFIRMED: scancel “is used to signal or cancel jobs, job arrays or job steps”; filters -u/--user, -t/--state, -n/--name, -p/--partition; combined filters must all match. Without --signal the whole job is terminated (SIGCONT, SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after KillWait). S scancel.html

Teaching point: scancel -u <me> kills all of the user’s jobs, not just the agent’s. Prefer scancel <jobid> for IDs the agent itself submitted.

CONFIRMED: Slurm can rate-limit RPCs per user (token bucket, since 23.02): short bursts allowed, “a sustained high rate of requests” restricted. S high_throughput.html. The page says nothing about polling squeue or job arrays vs many sbatch calls.
CONFIRMED (absence): Slurm quickstart says “All of the commands can run anywhere in the cluster” and does not define login nodes. No official Slurm page fetched covers login-node etiquette. S quickstart.html





UNCONFIRMED by Slurm docs; widely stated in site user guides. Login nodes are shared by all users; heavy work goes through sbatch/srun on compute nodes. Check your own site’s docs and cite them in the quest.
GENERAL PRACTICE, agent must not do on a login node: run pipelines or tools in the foreground (aligners, nextflow run as a long process unless site allows a head job), compress/index big files, find / or recursive grep -r over project/scratch trees, du -sh over millions of files, loops that call squeue every second, watch squeue, build large conda envs, run Jupyter or the agent’s test suite at scale.
GENERAL PRACTICE, OK on a login node: edit text, git, ls of one dir, squeue -u $USER, sbatch, scancel <id>, head/tail/wc on a log, sinfo.
GENERAL PRACTICE: use sbatch for batch work, srun --pty or salloc for interactive debugging, always set --time, --mem, --cpus-per-task. Use job arrays rather than looping sbatch (array vs loop load not covered by the Slurm page above).
Repo note: a local skill hpc-cluster-safety already exists in this environment; reuse its rules for quest text rather than inventing new ones.





UNCONFIRMED in official docs: network filesystems (Lustre, GPFS, NFS) degrade for everyone under metadata-heavy load (huge directory listings, find, grep -r, many small files). Agents explore by grep/glob, so scope searches to one subdirectory; never start at /, $HOME or a whole project root.
CONFIRMED: Claude Code runs its own file tools (Glob, Grep, Read) and bundled ripgrep; Read of a notebook over 256 KB errors and over 100 MB is refused. C tools-reference (a Read cap, not a filesystem-load control)
CONFIRMED: Claude Code keeps sessions, settings, plugins in ~/.claude; CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR relocates them (“stores your settings, session history, and plugins there instead”). Also writes ~/.claude.json (account details, MCP configs, trust decisions). C settings
GENERAL PRACTICE inference: if $HOME is shared/NFS-mounted across nodes, session history and transcripts (which can contain pasted data or paths) live on shared storage. Check permissions (chmod 700 ~/.claude) and whether home is backed up or readable by group. Not stated in docs.





CONFIRMED: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is sent as X-Api-Key; when set it overrides a subscription login; in -p mode it is always used; interactive mode asks once to approve. C env-vars
CONFIRMED: settings files: user ~/.claude/settings.json, project .claude/settings.json (commit it), local .claude/settings.local.json (kept out of git when Claude creates it; add to .gitignore if created by hand), managed. Precedence: managed > command line > local > shared project > user. Permission lists merge across files. C settings
CONFIRMED: deny precedes ask precedes allow; first match wins. Example in docs: "deny": ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)"]. C settings, C permissions
CONFIRMED: sandbox default reads cover “Most of the machine, including credential files such as ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials”. Use Read(...) deny rules or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead for key files. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: sandbox settings include credentials.files / credentials.envVars keys (purpose not read in detail). UNCONFIRMED what they do. C sandboxing
GENERAL PRACTICE: never put a key in a script or .claude/settings.json that is committed; for shared accounts prefer a per-user key from a file with mode 600, not a lab-wide key in a shared dir. The apiKeyHelper setting is named in the settings page; its behaviour was not read. UNCONFIRMED.
OpenCode: UNCONFIRMED where it stores keys (global config path not given on the permissions page). O permissions





CONFIRMED: “The sandbox runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2. On native Windows, Claude Code runs commands unsandboxed.” C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: Linux needs packages bubblewrap (filesystem isolation) and socat (network relay): sudo apt-get install bubblewrap socat or dnf. Ripgrep is bundled. Seccomp filter optional (Unix-socket blocking). C sandboxing

Teaching point: on a cluster you typically cannot sudo; a site must provide bwrap/socat or the sandbox cannot start. Whether bwrap works under a cluster’s user-namespace policy is UNCONFIRMED (site-specific).

CONFIRMED: fail-open by default: if unsupported or the dependency check fails, “Claude Code runs commands without sandboxing”; set sandbox.failIfUnavailable: true to exit instead. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: sandbox covers shell commands only; “Claude’s file tools, MCP servers, and hooks run outside it”. Writes allowed to working dir, per-user temp dir, added dirs. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: Claude can retry a failed command with dangerouslyDisableSandbox unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is false. excludedCommands run with no filesystem or network restrictions. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: plain ssh, most database drivers and UDP tools ignore the proxy and cannot reach allowed hosts. So ssh cluster from inside a sandbox does not work as a hop; run Claude Code on the cluster or outside the sandbox. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: bypassPermissions “Only use this mode in isolated environments like containers or VMs”; disable with permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable". C permissions
CONFIRMED: sandbox does not run Docker; docker needs excludedCommands. Apptainer/Singularity not mentioned; UNCONFIRMED.





GENERAL PRACTICE / UNCONFIRMED: many sites give compute nodes no or restricted internet; login nodes often have it. An agent running on a compute node may not reach the model API. Typical pattern: agent on login node or laptop, writes scripts, submits jobs; jobs run offline with pre-staged containers/data. Ask your site.
CONFIRMED: sandbox proxy checks each host against network.allowedDomains (starts empty); outside the list: prompt in manual/acceptEdits, refused in dontAsk, allowed without prompt in bypassPermissions. deniedDomains refused in every mode. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 disables auto-updates, telemetry, error reporting and feedback traffic; useful on restricted networks. C env-vars. Proxy variables (HTTPS_PROXY) rows not read: UNCONFIRMED here.





CONFIRMED: Claude Code “charges by API token consumption”; average about $13 per developer per active day, $150-250 per month, under $30 per day for 90% of users (enterprise averages). C costs
CONFIRMED: full conversation is sent with every request, each tool use sends another request; long sessions cost more; verbose tool output (logs) inflates context. Docs example: a hook that greps ERROR from a log “reducing context from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds”. C costs
CONFIRMED: BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS default 120000 (2 min), BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS default 600000 (10 min) for foreground commands. So foreground commands over 10 min are cut off by default; an agent waiting on srun or a polling loop hits this. C env-vars
CONFIRMED: scheduled/looped tasks “fire on its interval even while the session is idle, sending your full context each time”. Do not /loop a squeue poll. C costs
Scheduler side: no doc found that quantifies a safe squeue polling rate; Slurm RPC rate limiting exists (A1). GENERAL PRACTICE: poll at minutes, not seconds; use sacct or job output files instead.





UNCONFIRMED by docs: check institutional policy before sending cluster data, paths, logs or code to an external model API. Human genomic, clinical or controlled-access data (dbGaP, EGA-style agreements) often forbids third-party processing. Agent reads file contents into the model context; Read of any file within the working dir needs no approval (C permissions: file reads and Grep “No, within the working directory”).
CONFIRMED: Read is auto-approved inside the working dir and added dirs, so a project dir with controlled data is readable by the agent unless a Read(...) deny rule or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead covers it. C permissions, C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: organisations can enforce managed settings that user files cannot override. C settings
GENERAL PRACTICE: keep controlled data outside the agent’s working dir; give the agent synthetic or de-identified test data; ask the data owner and cluster admins first.





CONFIRMED: Bash rules: Bash(sbatch *) in ask forces a prompt; deny > ask > allow; an ask rule prompts even if a narrower allow matches. C permissions
CONFIRMED: ask/deny apply to any subcommand of a compound command (&&, ||, ;, |, &, newlines), including in for loops and $(...). C permissions
CONFIRMED limit: Bash deny/ask rules “isn’t a security boundary”: Bash(rm *) does not stop /bin/rm or bash -c 'rm ...'; Bash(git push *) does not stop git -C . push. For enforcement use sandboxing or a PreToolUse hook. C permissions
CONFIRMED: allow rules are not stripped past env-var wrappers or runners such as docker exec, npx: write exact inner-command rules. timeout, nice, nohup, time, stdbuf are stripped. C permissions
Suggested teaching config (derived from the above, not copied from docs):

allow: Bash(squeue *), Bash(sinfo *), Bash(sacct *)
ask: Bash(sbatch *), Bash(srun *), Bash(salloc *), Bash(scancel *)
deny: Bash(scancel -u *) (and scancel --user*), though bypassable per the caveat above
Teach: review the script and resource request (--time, --mem, array size) before approving sbatch; --test-only is a dry run.

OpenCode: CONFIRMED values allow, deny, ask; unmatched action = ask; ordered rules in opencode.jsonc, e.g. { "action": "shell", "resource": "git push *", "effect": "deny" } (V2 name shell, V1 bash); policies key for hard denials. BUT default base policy starts with { "action": "*", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" } (only .env reads ask), and “no rule asks for external_directory”. So OpenCode needs explicit ask rules for sbatch. O permissions (page version appears to be V2; check your installed version)





CONFIRMED: notebook is a JSON document (metadata, nbformat, nbformat_minor, cells); display_data stores image/png as base64; code cells carry execution_count and metadata. Source/output strings may be stored as lists of strings. https://nbformat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/format_description.html (2026-11-16)
Derived: a one-line code change also changes execution_count, outputs and embedded base64 images, so git diffs are dominated by JSON noise. Not stated as such in the docs.





CONFIRMED nbstripout: “strips output and some metadata”; keeps outputs on disk, only Git sees the cleaned version. nbstripout --install writes the filter to .git/config and attributes to .git/info/attributes; --attributes=.gitattributes to version the attributes. Git cannot set up filters on clone (“by design”), so each collaborator must run it. Limits: conflicts on pull/merge with non-stripped local changes; pre-commit mode modifies working copy. https://github.com/kynan/nbstripout
CONFIRMED jupytext: stores notebooks as Markdown or scripts for “clear and meaningful diffs when doing version control”; py:percent recommended for code; paired notebooks = .ipynb + .py of the same notebook, outputs stay in .ipynb, .py holds inputs. https://github.com/mwouts/jupytext (the readthedocs pages returned empty; README only)
CONFIRMED nbdime: nbdiff (terminal), nbdiff-web (browser), git integration via nbdime config-git --enable --global, merge driver keeps conflicted notebooks valid, nbdime mergetool. https://nbdime.readthedocs.io/en/latest/
CONFIRMED marimo: “Every marimo notebook is stored as pure Python (Git-friendly)”; reactive execution: “Delete a cell and marimo scrubs its variables from program memory, eliminating hidden state”; run as script with python your_notebook.py; convert: marimo convert your_notebook.ipynb > your_notebook.py. https://docs.marimo.io/
UNCONFIRMED: whether marimo’s .py stays fully deterministic when cells have side effects; and marimo-specific agent integration (not researched).





CONFIRMED: NotebookEdit “modifies a Jupyter notebook one cell at a time, targeting cells by their cell_id”; modes replace (default), insert, delete; not string replacement; refuses non-UTF-8 files; requires permission (listed “Yes”). C tools-reference
CONFIRMED: permission rules use the Edit(...) path format; Edit(notebooks/**) covers NotebookEdit. C tools-reference
CONFIRMED: replacing a code cell clears its execution count and saved outputs; to get outputs back, re-run the cell and dependents. C tools-reference
CONFIRMED: Read on .ipynb returns all cells with outputs (code, markdown, visualizations); error if cells exceed 256 KB or the token limit; notebook over 100 MB refused. Notebooks need a prior read on every model. C tools-reference
Derived (matches the above): agent never executes cells via NotebookEdit; outputs it edits are stale or empty until a human or jupyter nbconvert --execute re-runs. Reading output-heavy notebooks floods context (see A7). Strip outputs before pointing an agent at a notebook (nbstripout) or give it the jupytext .py.





Review agent-edited notebooks as text: pair with jupytext .py or use nbdiff; review the diff of source cells only; check git diff --stat for stray outputs/images.
Reproducibility: Restart Kernel and Run All, top to bottom, before commit; out-of-order cells and deleted cells leave hidden state in the kernel (marimo’s design removes this per its docs, B2). An agent that replaces a cell clears outputs (B3), so a green-looking notebook can be stale.
Run headless in CI or a cluster job, not an interactive Jupyter on the login node (see A2).
Pin environments: container or lockfile; the agent should not pip install into a shared env.




Source: https://github.com/NBISweden/claude-skills/pull/10 , file plugins/nbis-safety/skills/hpc-cluster-safety/SKILL.md. This is the site owner’s own practice (a maintainers’ skill, not vendor docs). Nothing run. Quest text treats it as “General practice” unless a Slurm man page below confirms it. Site names in the source are deliberately not repeated; the quests stay generic. - Maintainers’ practice (General practice): agents on login nodes may be barred by site policy (then use an interactive compute allocation; ask staff); scope filesystem operations (no broad find/du/ls --recursive/grep --recursive, no ls --format=long or wide globs on big directories, avoid many small files); poll no faster than about once a minute, one loop, scoped; prefer sbatch --parsable --wait or the pipeline’s poller; never resubmit because a wait timed out, check State with sacct; arrays with a concurrency cap; ask where scratch is, not /tmp, $TMPDIR set proves nothing; stay inside the project’s paths; do not assume Slurm; compare request, allocation and use with sacct; rsync --dry-run --itemize-changes before copy, list before rm, large transfers via scheduler or a data-transfer node; stricter project instructions (AGENTS.md) win over the skill; prefer long options; do not trust “a few seconds”, ask. - CONFIRMED (Slurm man pages, read 2026-11-17, version shown on page 26.05): - squeue.html: running it “from loops” can degrade slurmctld (possible denial of service); --user and a single job ID via --jobs improve performance on large systems. - sacct.html: “Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure calls to slurmdbd from loops.” States include OUT_OF_MEMORY (“Job experienced out of memory error”); ExitCode has the signal number after a colon. - sbatch.html: --parsable prints only the job ID (and cluster name if present). --wait: “Do not exit until the submitted job terminates”; sbatch’s exit code equals the job’s; signal-terminated gives 1; arrays give the highest task code. --array=0-15%4 limits simultaneous tasks to 4. --mem-per-cpu above MaxMemPerCPU is reduced and --cpus-per-task is raised to compensate (the page also notes --mem handling; the exact --mem above CPUs x limit behaviour and the 0:125 / 137 exit codes were not confirmed on these pages: UNCONFIRMED, treated as maintainers’ practice). - scancel.html: other bulk selectors besides --user: --me (“jobs owned by the current user”), --name, --state (PENDING, RUNNING or SUSPENDED), --partition, also --account, --qos, --reservation, --wckey, --nodelist; combined filters must all match. The page does not say which version added --me. - NOT CHECKED: scontrol show partition, MaxMemPerCPU, TRESBillingWeights, EnforcePartLimits claims (scontrol/slurm.conf pages not fetched).

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
CONFIRMED: sbatch “is used to submit a job script for later execution”; srun “to submit a job for execution or initiate job steps in real time”; squeue “reports the state of jobs or job steps”; scancel “to cancel a pending or running job or job step”; sinfo reports partitions and nodes. S quickstart.html (2026-11-16)
CONFIRMED: sbatch “exits immediately after the script is successfully transferred to the Slurm controller and assigned a Slurm job ID”. Default time limit “is the partition’s default time limit”. --test-only validates and estimates start, “No job is actually submitted”. --parsable prints only the job ID. S sbatch.html
CONFIRMED: “If necessary, srun will first create a resource allocation in which to run the parallel job.” So srun outside an allocation requests resources and (by default) runs synchronously. S srun.html (first 100k of 175k chars read; --pty entry not read)
CONFIRMED: scancel “is used to signal or cancel jobs, job arrays or job steps”; filters -u/--user, -t/--state, -n/--name, -p/--partition; combined filters must all match. Without --signal the whole job is terminated (SIGCONT, SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after KillWait). S scancel.html

Teaching point: scancel -u <me> kills all of the user’s jobs, not just the agent’s. Prefer scancel <jobid> for IDs the agent itself submitted.

CONFIRMED: Slurm can rate-limit RPCs per user (token bucket, since 23.02): short bursts allowed, “a sustained high rate of requests” restricted. S high_throughput.html. The page says nothing about polling squeue or job arrays vs many sbatch calls.
CONFIRMED (absence): Slurm quickstart says “All of the commands can run anywhere in the cluster” and does not define login nodes. No official Slurm page fetched covers login-node etiquette. S quickstart.html

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
UNCONFIRMED by Slurm docs; widely stated in site user guides. Login nodes are shared by all users; heavy work goes through sbatch/srun on compute nodes. Check your own site’s docs and cite them in the quest.
GENERAL PRACTICE, agent must not do on a login node: run pipelines or tools in the foreground (aligners, nextflow run as a long process unless site allows a head job), compress/index big files, find / or recursive grep -r over project/scratch trees, du -sh over millions of files, loops that call squeue every second, watch squeue, build large conda envs, run Jupyter or the agent’s test suite at scale.
GENERAL PRACTICE, OK on a login node: edit text, git, ls of one dir, squeue -u $USER, sbatch, scancel <id>, head/tail/wc on a log, sinfo.
GENERAL PRACTICE: use sbatch for batch work, srun --pty or salloc for interactive debugging, always set --time, --mem, --cpus-per-task. Use job arrays rather than looping sbatch (array vs loop load not covered by the Slurm page above).
Repo note: a local skill hpc-cluster-safety already exists in this environment; reuse its rules for quest text rather than inventing new ones.

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
UNCONFIRMED in official docs: network filesystems (Lustre, GPFS, NFS) degrade for everyone under metadata-heavy load (huge directory listings, find, grep -r, many small files). Agents explore by grep/glob, so scope searches to one subdirectory; never start at /, $HOME or a whole project root.
CONFIRMED: Claude Code runs its own file tools (Glob, Grep, Read) and bundled ripgrep; Read of a notebook over 256 KB errors and over 100 MB is refused. C tools-reference (a Read cap, not a filesystem-load control)
CONFIRMED: Claude Code keeps sessions, settings, plugins in ~/.claude; CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR relocates them (“stores your settings, session history, and plugins there instead”). Also writes ~/.claude.json (account details, MCP configs, trust decisions). C settings
GENERAL PRACTICE inference: if $HOME is shared/NFS-mounted across nodes, session history and transcripts (which can contain pasted data or paths) live on shared storage. Check permissions (chmod 700 ~/.claude) and whether home is backed up or readable by group. Not stated in docs.

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
CONFIRMED: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is sent as X-Api-Key; when set it overrides a subscription login; in -p mode it is always used; interactive mode asks once to approve. C env-vars
CONFIRMED: settings files: user ~/.claude/settings.json, project .claude/settings.json (commit it), local .claude/settings.local.json (kept out of git when Claude creates it; add to .gitignore if created by hand), managed. Precedence: managed > command line > local > shared project > user. Permission lists merge across files. C settings
CONFIRMED: deny precedes ask precedes allow; first match wins. Example in docs: "deny": ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)"]. C settings, C permissions
CONFIRMED: sandbox default reads cover “Most of the machine, including credential files such as ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials”. Use Read(...) deny rules or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead for key files. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: sandbox settings include credentials.files / credentials.envVars keys (purpose not read in detail). UNCONFIRMED what they do. C sandboxing
GENERAL PRACTICE: never put a key in a script or .claude/settings.json that is committed; for shared accounts prefer a per-user key from a file with mode 600, not a lab-wide key in a shared dir. The apiKeyHelper setting is named in the settings page; its behaviour was not read. UNCONFIRMED.
OpenCode: UNCONFIRMED where it stores keys (global config path not given on the permissions page). O permissions

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
CONFIRMED: “The sandbox runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2. On native Windows, Claude Code runs commands unsandboxed.” C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: Linux needs packages bubblewrap (filesystem isolation) and socat (network relay): sudo apt-get install bubblewrap socat or dnf. Ripgrep is bundled. Seccomp filter optional (Unix-socket blocking). C sandboxing

Teaching point: on a cluster you typically cannot sudo; a site must provide bwrap/socat or the sandbox cannot start. Whether bwrap works under a cluster’s user-namespace policy is UNCONFIRMED (site-specific).

CONFIRMED: fail-open by default: if unsupported or the dependency check fails, “Claude Code runs commands without sandboxing”; set sandbox.failIfUnavailable: true to exit instead. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: sandbox covers shell commands only; “Claude’s file tools, MCP servers, and hooks run outside it”. Writes allowed to working dir, per-user temp dir, added dirs. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: Claude can retry a failed command with dangerouslyDisableSandbox unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is false. excludedCommands run with no filesystem or network restrictions. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: plain ssh, most database drivers and UDP tools ignore the proxy and cannot reach allowed hosts. So ssh cluster from inside a sandbox does not work as a hop; run Claude Code on the cluster or outside the sandbox. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: bypassPermissions “Only use this mode in isolated environments like containers or VMs”; disable with permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable". C permissions
CONFIRMED: sandbox does not run Docker; docker needs excludedCommands. Apptainer/Singularity not mentioned; UNCONFIRMED.

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
GENERAL PRACTICE / UNCONFIRMED: many sites give compute nodes no or restricted internet; login nodes often have it. An agent running on a compute node may not reach the model API. Typical pattern: agent on login node or laptop, writes scripts, submits jobs; jobs run offline with pre-staged containers/data. Ask your site.
CONFIRMED: sandbox proxy checks each host against network.allowedDomains (starts empty); outside the list: prompt in manual/acceptEdits, refused in dontAsk, allowed without prompt in bypassPermissions. deniedDomains refused in every mode. C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 disables auto-updates, telemetry, error reporting and feedback traffic; useful on restricted networks. C env-vars. Proxy variables (HTTPS_PROXY) rows not read: UNCONFIRMED here.

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
CONFIRMED: Claude Code “charges by API token consumption”; average about $13 per developer per active day, $150-250 per month, under $30 per day for 90% of users (enterprise averages). C costs
CONFIRMED: full conversation is sent with every request, each tool use sends another request; long sessions cost more; verbose tool output (logs) inflates context. Docs example: a hook that greps ERROR from a log “reducing context from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds”. C costs
CONFIRMED: BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS default 120000 (2 min), BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS default 600000 (10 min) for foreground commands. So foreground commands over 10 min are cut off by default; an agent waiting on srun or a polling loop hits this. C env-vars
CONFIRMED: scheduled/looped tasks “fire on its interval even while the session is idle, sending your full context each time”. Do not /loop a squeue poll. C costs
Scheduler side: no doc found that quantifies a safe squeue polling rate; Slurm RPC rate limiting exists (A1). GENERAL PRACTICE: poll at minutes, not seconds; use sacct or job output files instead.

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
UNCONFIRMED by docs: check institutional policy before sending cluster data, paths, logs or code to an external model API. Human genomic, clinical or controlled-access data (dbGaP, EGA-style agreements) often forbids third-party processing. Agent reads file contents into the model context; Read of any file within the working dir needs no approval (C permissions: file reads and Grep “No, within the working directory”).
CONFIRMED: Read is auto-approved inside the working dir and added dirs, so a project dir with controlled data is readable by the agent unless a Read(...) deny rule or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead covers it. C permissions, C sandboxing
CONFIRMED: organisations can enforce managed settings that user files cannot override. C settings
GENERAL PRACTICE: keep controlled data outside the agent’s working dir; give the agent synthetic or de-identified test data; ask the data owner and cluster admins first.

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
CONFIRMED: Bash rules: Bash(sbatch *) in ask forces a prompt; deny > ask > allow; an ask rule prompts even if a narrower allow matches. C permissions
CONFIRMED: ask/deny apply to any subcommand of a compound command (&&, ||, ;, |, &, newlines), including in for loops and $(...). C permissions
CONFIRMED limit: Bash deny/ask rules “isn’t a security boundary”: Bash(rm *) does not stop /bin/rm or bash -c 'rm ...'; Bash(git push *) does not stop git -C . push. For enforcement use sandboxing or a PreToolUse hook. C permissions
CONFIRMED: allow rules are not stripped past env-var wrappers or runners such as docker exec, npx: write exact inner-command rules. timeout, nice, nohup, time, stdbuf are stripped. C permissions
Suggested teaching config (derived from the above, not copied from docs):

allow: Bash(squeue *), Bash(sinfo *), Bash(sacct *)
ask: Bash(sbatch *), Bash(srun *), Bash(salloc *), Bash(scancel *)
deny: Bash(scancel -u *) (and scancel --user*), though bypassable per the caveat above
Teach: review the script and resource request (--time, --mem, array size) before approving sbatch; --test-only is a dry run.

OpenCode: CONFIRMED values allow, deny, ask; unmatched action = ask; ordered rules in opencode.jsonc, e.g. { "action": "shell", "resource": "git push *", "effect": "deny" } (V2 name shell, V1 bash); policies key for hard denials. BUT default base policy starts with { "action": "*", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" } (only .env reads ask), and “no rule asks for external_directory”. So OpenCode needs explicit ask rules for sbatch. O permissions (page version appears to be V2; check your installed version)

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
CONFIRMED: notebook is a JSON document (metadata, nbformat, nbformat_minor, cells); display_data stores image/png as base64; code cells carry execution_count and metadata. Source/output strings may be stored as lists of strings. https://nbformat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/format_description.html (2026-11-16)
Derived: a one-line code change also changes execution_count, outputs and embedded base64 images, so git diffs are dominated by JSON noise. Not stated as such in the docs.

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
CONFIRMED nbstripout: “strips output and some metadata”; keeps outputs on disk, only Git sees the cleaned version. nbstripout --install writes the filter to .git/config and attributes to .git/info/attributes; --attributes=.gitattributes to version the attributes. Git cannot set up filters on clone (“by design”), so each collaborator must run it. Limits: conflicts on pull/merge with non-stripped local changes; pre-commit mode modifies working copy. https://github.com/kynan/nbstripout
CONFIRMED jupytext: stores notebooks as Markdown or scripts for “clear and meaningful diffs when doing version control”; py:percent recommended for code; paired notebooks = .ipynb + .py of the same notebook, outputs stay in .ipynb, .py holds inputs. https://github.com/mwouts/jupytext (the readthedocs pages returned empty; README only)
CONFIRMED nbdime: nbdiff (terminal), nbdiff-web (browser), git integration via nbdime config-git --enable --global, merge driver keeps conflicted notebooks valid, nbdime mergetool. https://nbdime.readthedocs.io/en/latest/
CONFIRMED marimo: “Every marimo notebook is stored as pure Python (Git-friendly)”; reactive execution: “Delete a cell and marimo scrubs its variables from program memory, eliminating hidden state”; run as script with python your_notebook.py; convert: marimo convert your_notebook.ipynb > your_notebook.py. https://docs.marimo.io/
UNCONFIRMED: whether marimo’s .py stays fully deterministic when cells have side effects; and marimo-specific agent integration (not researched).

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
CONFIRMED: NotebookEdit “modifies a Jupyter notebook one cell at a time, targeting cells by their cell_id”; modes replace (default), insert, delete; not string replacement; refuses non-UTF-8 files; requires permission (listed “Yes”). C tools-reference
CONFIRMED: permission rules use the Edit(...) path format; Edit(notebooks/**) covers NotebookEdit. C tools-reference
CONFIRMED: replacing a code cell clears its execution count and saved outputs; to get outputs back, re-run the cell and dependents. C tools-reference
CONFIRMED: Read on .ipynb returns all cells with outputs (code, markdown, visualizations); error if cells exceed 256 KB or the token limit; notebook over 100 MB refused. Notebooks need a prior read on every model. C tools-reference
Derived (matches the above): agent never executes cells via NotebookEdit; outputs it edits are stale or empty until a human or jupyter nbconvert --execute re-runs. Reading output-heavy notebooks floods context (see A7). Strip outputs before pointing an agent at a notebook (nbstripout) or give it the jupytext .py.

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text:
Review agent-edited notebooks as text: pair with jupytext .py or use nbdiff; review the diff of source cells only; check git diff --stat for stray outputs/images.
Reproducibility: Restart Kernel and Run All, top to bottom, before commit; out-of-order cells and deleted cells leave hidden state in the kernel (marimo’s design removes this per its docs, B2). An agent that replaces a cell clears outputs (B3), so a green-looking notebook can be stale.
Run headless in CI or a cluster job, not an interactive Jupyter on the login node (see A2).
Pin environments: container or lockfile; the agent should not pip install into a shared env.

title: HPC safety and notebooks with coding agents
text: Source: https://github.com/NBISweden/claude-skills/pull/10 , file plugins/nbis-safety/skills/hpc-cluster-safety/SKILL.md. This is the site owner’s own practice (a maintainers’ skill, not vendor docs). Nothing run. Quest text treats it as “General practice” unless a Slurm man page below confirms it. Site names in the source are deliberately not repeated; the quests stay generic. - Maintainers’ practice (General practice): agents on login nodes may be barred by site policy (then use an interactive compute allocation; ask staff); scope filesystem operations (no broad find/du/ls --recursive/grep --recursive, no ls --format=long or wide globs on big directories, avoid many small files); poll no faster than about once a minute, one loop, scoped; prefer sbatch --parsable --wait or the pipeline’s poller; never resubmit because a wait timed out, check State with sacct; arrays with a concurrency cap; ask where scratch is, not /tmp, $TMPDIR set proves nothing; stay inside the project’s paths; do not assume Slurm; compare request, allocation and use with sacct; rsync --dry-run --itemize-changes before copy, list before rm, large transfers via scheduler or a data-transfer node; stricter project instructions (AGENTS.md) win over the skill; prefer long options; do not trust “a few seconds”, ask. - CONFIRMED (Slurm man pages, read 2026-11-17, version shown on page 26.05): - squeue.html: running it “from loops” can degrade slurmctld (possible denial of service); --user and a single job ID via --jobs improve performance on large systems. - sacct.html: “Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure calls to slurmdbd from loops.” States include OUT_OF_MEMORY (“Job experienced out of memory error”); ExitCode has the signal number after a colon. - sbatch.html: --parsable prints only the job ID (and cluster name if present). --wait: “Do not exit until the submitted job terminates”; sbatch’s exit code equals the job’s; signal-terminated gives 1; arrays give the highest task code. --array=0-15%4 limits simultaneous tasks to 4. --mem-per-cpu above MaxMemPerCPU is reduced and --cpus-per-task is raised to compensate (the page also notes --mem handling; the exact --mem above CPUs x limit behaviour and the 0:125 / 137 exit codes were not confirmed on these pages: UNCONFIRMED, treated as maintainers’ practice). - scancel.html: other bulk selectors besides --user: --me (“jobs owned by the current user”), --name, --state (PENDING, RUNNING or SUSPENDED), --partition, also --account, --qos, --reservation, --wckey, --nodelist; combined filters must all match. The page does not say which version added --me. - NOT CHECKED: scontrol show partition, MaxMemPerCPU, TRESBillingWeights, EnforcePartLimits claims (scontrol/slurm.conf pages not fetched).

title: Forge zone: skills, skill evals, plugins, OpenCode, trust
text:
Read 2026-11-13. Official docs only. Local claude --version: 2.1.325. Docs pages show no publish date; skills page cites versions up to v2.1.319. Method: pages fetched via a summarising fetch tool (quotes as returned). Base: C = https://code.claude.com/docs/en/ ; O = https://opencode.ai/docs/ Decision fed: accuracy of quest text for Skills -> Evals -> Plugins -> OpenCode -> Security.



CONFIRMED: project skill path .claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md (“loads in sessions in this repository”); personal ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md. C skills
CONFIRMED: “All fields are optional. Only description is recommended.” Smallest skill = frontmatter with description: + a body. Dir name becomes /<name> unless name is set. C skills
CONFIRMED: edits under .claude/skills/ are picked up without restart; a top-level skills dir created mid-session needs /reload-skills. C skills
CONFIRMED: confirm pickup by typing / (menu), running /skills, then asking something matching the description. claude --debug + search [names] for refused names. C skills
CONFIRMED: /skill-doctor shows skills in the listing but never invoked; /doctor for setup check. C skills
CONFIRMED reasons it does not trigger (all from C skills):

Frontmatter only read if opening --- is the file’s first line.
YAML that fails to parse: skill loads with no fields set.
Misspelled field names ignored silently.
description+when_to_use truncated at 1,536 chars in the listing; put key use case first.
disable-model-invocation: true means Claude cannot invoke it itself.
Names with zero-width/control chars or </> refused.
Skills in subdirectories load only after Claude touches a file there.

UNCONFIRMED: the page’s own “Skill not triggering” troubleshooting section (last ~19.5k chars of the page were not read). Re-read with offset 100000 before quoting.





CONFIRMED: claude plugin eval [target] [options]; requires Claude Code v2.1.269+, git 2.31+ if git installed. C plugin-evals, C plugins/cli-reference#plugin-eval
CONFIRMED: target is a plugin dir (.), a single prompt.md/case.yaml, or installed name[@marketplace]/name@skills-dir. A skills-directory plugin (folder with .claude-plugin/plugin.json) qualifies. A bare .claude/skills/x/SKILL.md with no manifest is not stated to qualify. C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED layout: evals/<case>/prompt.md (frontmatter = run fields, body = prompt), evals/<case>/graders/<name>.md (frontmatter type + options), optional case.yaml, evals/results/<timestamp>/{aggregate-result.json,report.html}. A case with no grader fails to load. claude plugin eval init --bare <name> writes a blank case. C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED prompt.md fields: max_turns (10), timeout_seconds (300), runs (3), model, allowed_tools, tags, env (EVAL_* only). C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED six grader types: regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists (free, computed from transcript/files); llm, baseline (judge model, cost). “There are no custom-code graders.” C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED skill-fired grader: type: tool_used, tool: Skill, input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?your-skill-name"'; passes if invoked at least once. tool_used has min/max (min: 0, max: 0 = never called). C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED scoring: 3 runs per case per arm; run score = fraction of graders passed; case passes when mean >= --threshold (default 1.0). Default also runs a no-plugin arm: WITH, W/OUT, Δ. tool_used: Skill is excluded from score in two-arm runs (indicator only) unless arm: both. C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED flags: --runs, --case <glob>, --tag, --model, --judge-model, --ablation none|with-without, --threshold, --max-cost-usd, --allow-tools, --scaffold, --trust-plugin, --mocks, --json [path], --output-dir, --no-publish, --keep-temp, --eval-dir. Iterate cheaply: claude plugin eval . --case <name> --runs 1 --ablation none. C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED exit codes: 0 pass; 1 below threshold/load failure/untrusted/API error; 2 partial (cost ceiling or auth); 130 interrupted; 143 terminated. C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED cost: “Every eval run and every judge grader is a real model call on your account”; cost shown is a list-price estimate. About cases x runs x 2 arms agent runs, plus 3 judge calls per llm/baseline grader per run. C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED isolation: each run is a claude -p child with temp home/cwd/config, only the plugin loaded; no user settings, CLAUDE.md, MCP, other plugins; case files hidden from agent. Read-only tools only unless granted; granting Bash runs it under the OS sandbox (writes confined to workspace, network limited); with no sandbox backend (native Windows) runs are refused. First run asks “Trust this plugin directory?”. C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED guidance: phrase prompts as a user would, not naming the skill; pair one result grader with one process grader (tool_used/tool_order); use regex on files for long output, llm only for short output with concrete PASS/FAIL rubric; pin --model/--judge-model in CI. C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED: Δ near zero with failing tool_used: Skill “usually a real finding”: the description does not trigger on that phrasing. C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED: claude plugin validate checks syntax/schema, not behavior. C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED: skill-creator plugin has a separate evals/evals.json format; neither tool reads the other’s cases. C plugin-evals





CONFIRMED: plugin = directory of skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers etc. loaded as one unit; manifest optional, at .claude-plugin/plugin.json. C plugins (overview), C plugins/manifest-reference
CONFIRMED manifest: only name required (kebab-case; namespaces components, e.g. /my-first-plugin:hello). Others: displayName, version (pins updates), description, author{name,email,url}, homepage, repository, license, keywords, defaultEnabled, dependencies, userConfig, skills, commands, agents, hooks, mcpServers, lspServers, outputStyles, workflows, experimental.{themes,monitors,evals}. Names starting claude-/anthropic- are a validate error. C plugins/manifest-reference
CONFIRMED layout: skills/<name>/SKILL.md, commands/ (older; prefer skills), agents/*.md, hooks/hooks.json (top-level "hooks" key), .mcp.json, .lsp.json, bin/, output-styles/. Only plugin.json goes inside .claude-plugin/; components there do not load. C manifest-reference
CONFIRMED local test without marketplace: claude --plugin-dir ./my-first-plugin; /reload-plugins after edits; /plugin Installed/Errors tabs; claude plugin list. CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS needs v2.1.280+. C plugins/create
CONFIRMED: claude plugin validate <path> [--strict] [--json]; exit 0 pass, 1 fail, 2 unexpected error. --strict fails on warnings. C plugins/cli-reference#plugin-validate, C manifest-reference
CONFIRMED subcommands listed: init, install, uninstall, enable, disable, update, list, details, configure, prune, eval, eval init, tag, test (mods), validate; plugin marketplace add|list|remove|update. claude plugins is an alias. C plugins/cli-reference
CONFIRMED marketplace: a repo/dir with .claude-plugin/marketplace.json listing plugins and where to fetch each; a catalog, not a hosted store. Add once (claude plugin marketplace add <source>), install by name (commit-commands@claude-plugins-official). Official marketplace auto-added on first interactive start. Install scopes: user, project, local. C plugins (overview)
CONFIRMED: claude plugin init <name> scaffolds under ~/.claude/skills/ (auto-loads as <name>@skills-dir). C plugins/create





CONFIRMED: OpenCode has plugins AND skills AND agents. O plugins, O skills, O agents
CONFIRMED plugins: code plugins (“add tools, hooks, integrations, commands, agents”); auto-load .ts/.js or package folders from .opencode/plugins/ (project) or ~/.config/opencode/plugins/ (global); or listed in config as npm packages (versioned/scoped), git repos, or local directories. O plugins
UNCONFIRMED: config key spelling. The fetched page example shows "plugins": [...]; I recall plugin (singular) from older docs. Check the page raw before teaching.
CONFIRMED skills: .opencode/skills, plus compat .claude/skills and .agents/skills (project); ~/.config/opencode/skills, ~/.claude/skills, ~/.agents/skills (global). Found as SKILL.md in dirs (or flat *.md). Skill ID comes from file path; name is display only; skills without description are not advertised. Model loads via skill tool; @skill-id in a prompt loads one yourself. Permissions allow|ask|deny on skill. O skills
CONFIRMED agents: markdown with frontmatter (body = system prompt) in .opencode/agents/<name>.md or ~/.config/opencode/agents/, or JSONC under agents. O agents
UNCONFIRMED: whether OpenCode reads Claude plugin .claude-plugin/plugin.json; docs read say nothing. Only plain .claude/skills is documented as compatible.
UNCONFIRMED: any OpenCode equivalent of claude plugin eval/validate (not looked for beyond the three pages).





CONFIRMED: “A Claude Code plugin you install can execute arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges.” Hooks, monitors, mods, stdio MCP/LSP servers and bin/ run; hooks/monitors/servers run outside the sandbox and permission rules. Skills/commands/agents enter context as instructions. C plugins/security
CONFIRMED: trust warning text: “Make sure you trust a plugin before installing, updating, or using it. Anthropic does not control what MCP servers, files, or other software are included in plugins…” C plugins/security
CONFIRMED review steps: claude plugin marketplace list (source); /plugin details pane “Will install”; read hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json, bin/; claude --plugin-dir <dir> plugin details <name> prints a Component inventory without a session. C plugins/security

CONFIRMED: target is a plugin dir (.), a single prompt.md/case.yaml, or installed name[@marketplace]/name@skills-dir. A skills-directory plugin (folder with .claude-plugin/plugin.json) qualifies. A bare .claude/skills/x/SKILL.md with no manifest is not stated to qualify. C plugin-evals
CONFIRMED layout: evals/<case>/prompt.md (frontmatter = run fields, body = prompt), evals/<case>/graders/<name>.md (frontmatter type + options), optional case.yaml, evals/results/<timestamp>/{aggregate-result.json,report.html}. A case with no grader fails to load. claude plugin eval init --bare <name> writes a blank case. C plugin-evals

title: Failure modes zone: memory, sessions, usage, context poisoning, LLM failure modes
text:
Checked 2026-11-16. Pages fetched via a summarising fetch tool (quotes as returned, short). Paraphrase on the site. Not repeated here: tokens, context window, compaction survival list, CLAUDE.md-as-user-message (see fundamentals.md, terminology.md). Base: C = https://code.claude.com/docs/en/ ; P = https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/ ; A = https://www.anthropic.com/



CONFIRMED: two memory systems, both loaded at the start of every session. CLAUDE.md = instructions you write; auto memory = notes Claude writes itself from your corrections and preferences. “Each Claude Code session begins with a fresh context window”; these two carry knowledge across sessions. C memory
CONFIRMED: CLAUDE.md scopes are project, user, or org. Auto memory is per git repository (all worktrees share it), machine-local, not shared across machines or cloud environments. C memory
CONFIRMED: auto memory lives in ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/, with a MEMORY.md index plus topic files; plain markdown you can read, edit or delete. Only the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md load at session start; topic files are read on demand. Memory files are exempt from the transcript retention sweep. C memory
CONFIRMED: /memory lists CLAUDE.md files and memory locations, toggles auto memory (autoMemoryEnabled), opens the memory folder. “Saved N memories” / “Recalled N memories” in the UI means Claude touched that directory. /context all lists Memory files that loaded. C memory, C commands
CONFIRMED: memory is “context, not enforced configuration”; contradictory instructions: “Claude may pick one arbitrarily”. /doctor prompt-audit checks instruction files for outdated or conflicting content. C memory
CONFIRMED difference from the context window: the context window is the live working space of one session and empties with /clear or a new session; memory is files on disk re-read into a new window. Memory files also occupy context every session. C how-claude-code-works, C memory
CONFIRMED (API): memory tool {"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"}, client-side: Claude requests file operations (view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, rename) under /memories, and your application executes them on storage you control. Purpose: persist info across conversations without keeping it all in the window. Developer must block path traversal. P agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool
Consequence (inference): memory is not truth, it is text that was once written; wrong entries get loaded forever (see section 4).





CONFIRMED: a session is “a saved conversation tied to a project directory”, stored locally as JSONL under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl; transcripts deleted after 30 days by default (cleanupPeriodDays). C sessions
CONFIRMED: “Sessions are independent”: a new session starts with a fresh context window and no history from earlier sessions. C how-claude-code-works
CONFIRMED commands: claude --continue (most recent in this directory), claude --resume [name|id] (picker), /resume inside a session, claude --continue --fork-session or /branch (copy into a new session ID), /rename, /clear [name] (new empty conversation; old one stays resumable; alias /new), /compact [instructions] (replace history with a summary; stays the same conversation), /context, /export. C sessions, C commands
CONFIRMED: resume restores messages, tool calls and results (from the last compaction summary onward if compacted), model and permission mode; it does not restore flags such as --mcp-config, --plugin-dir, --add-dir. C sessions
CONFIRMED: /clear keeps project memory (CLAUDE.md, auto memory) but drops the conversation. C commands (“Between sessions”)
Session vs memory (confirmed pieces combined): session = this conversation’s transcript (resumable, temporary, tied to a directory); memory = durable notes/instructions that every new session reads. Compaction shrinks a session; it does not create memory.





CONFIRMED: /usage shows session cost (computed locally from token counts at list price, an estimate), plan usage limits, activity stats; on Pro/Max/Ultra/Team/Enterprise also a breakdown of what counts against limits (skills, subagents, plugins, MCP servers) with recommendations. /cost is an alias of /usage; /stats is an alias opening the Stats tab. Session totals reset on /clear. C costs, C commands
CONFIRMED: for subscribers the dollar figure “isn’t relevant for billing”; the plan bars are what matter. Teams/Enterprise: a per-seat allowance with a rolling five-hour window and a weekly window, shared with Claude chat and Cowork. Messages “You’ve hit your session limit” / “weekly limit” are those windows; /usage-credits buys extra. C costs
CONFIRMED: /usage may say “rate limited until …” meaning only that Claude Code cannot fetch plan limits, “not that your work with Claude is limited”. C costs
CONFIRMED: API usage is billed per token; thinking tokens are billed as output tokens. C costs
CONFIRMED why usage climbs: Claude Code sends the whole conversation on every request, and each tool-using step is another request; with caching the history is re-read at the cheaper cached rate but a one-line question in an all-day session still draws on the whole conversation. First message after a break longer than the cache lifetime reprocesses everything. /compact itself reads the whole conversation (a large request). Also: scheduled /loop tasks firing while idle, subagents and agent teams (each its own context; teams about 7x a standard session), extended thinking. C costs
CONFIRMED large tool outputs: Claude “reading a 10,000-line log” is the docs’ own example; a hook can filter to matching lines so context drops from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds. Subagents keep verbose output in their own window; only a summary returns (but their requests still draw on usage). C costs
CONFIRMED mitigations: /clear between unrelated tasks (“costs nothing”), /compact <focus>, /context to see what fills the window, /model and /effort to match model and effort to the job, specific prompts, disable unused MCP servers with /mcp, keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines (move workflows into skills). C costs
UNCONFIRMED: the exact token size of the plan allowance on Pro/Max; docs point to claude.com/pricing and the Help Center. Do not state numbers.





COMMUNITY TERM, not vendor documentation. Coined in “How Long Contexts Fail” by Drew Breunig, 2025-06-22 (author name taken from the O’Reilly reprint listing / my search; the fetched page text did not name him; confirm). https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/22/how-contexts-fail-and-how-to-fix-them.html

Poisoning: a hallucination or other error enters the context and is repeatedly referenced. His example: the Gemini 2.5 technical report’s Pokemon-playing agent, whose recorded goals/summary became corrupted with false game state, so it fixated on impossible goals.
Same post, also COMMUNITY TERMS: distraction (context so long the model over-focuses on it and neglects what training taught), confusion (superfluous content degrades the answer), clash (new info or tools contradict earlier context).
CONFIRMED that the fetched post gives no poisoning-specific fix (promises a follow-up on quarantine and dynamic tool loading). Mitigations below are Anthropic’s, or our inference, not his.

CONFIRMED official adjacent language: Anthropic’s context engineering article calls the buildup of stale or unneeded material “context pollution” and notes aggressive compaction can drop details that matter later. https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents (fetched; wording from summariser)
CONFIRMED official guidance that errors persist in the conversation: “If you’ve corrected the same thing twice and it’s still wrong, a third correction mostly adds to a conversation that already contains two failed attempts for Claude to keep re-reading. /clear plus one new prompt that folds in what you learned works better almost every time.” Also “after two failed corrections run /clear and write a better prompt.” C best-practices
CONFIRMED tools: /rewind (or Esc twice) rolls conversation and/or code back to an earlier prompt and can summarize stale parts; /clear; subagents isolate noisy work. C best-practices, C costs
Mitigations (inference built on the above): (1) fresh session with a short, corrected brief; (2) rewind to before the bad turn rather than arguing; (3) never let Claude write a claim into CLAUDE.md/MEMORY.md until you checked it against the source (poisoned memory is reloaded every session; open it via /memory, delete the line); (4) have the agent re-derive from files or a script, not from earlier chat; (5) use /doctor prompt-audit to find stale or contradictory instruction files.
UNCONFIRMED: any official Anthropic use of the term “context poisoning”.





Brief: a token is a chunk of text the model reads (word piece, character or byte); not a word. Usage and context limits are counted in tokens. Full detail and sources in fundamentals.md section 1.




Official hedge to quote in spirit: even advanced models “can sometimes generate text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the given context”; techniques “don’t eliminate them entirely. Always validate critical information.” P test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations



Looks like: plausible DOI or PMID that does not exist; a tool option that was never implemented; confident wrong sequence annotation.
CONFIRMED mitigations (same page): permit “I don’t know”; extract word-for-word quotes first for long documents (page suggests >20k tokens); make every claim cite a quote and retract any claim with none; run the prompt several times and compare (best-of-N); restrict to supplied documents.
Our advice (inference): look up every citation and ID in PubMed/Ensembl/the tool’s --help; the agent can run the tool to test a flag.





Looks like: agrees with your wrong hypothesis, softens a correct criticism when you push back, praises a flawed analysis.
CONFIRMED peer-reviewed: Sharma et al., “Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models”, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.13548 (Anthropic authors). Five RLHF assistants (incl. claude-1.3, claude-2.0) often match a user’s stated view; human and preference-model raters sometimes prefer convincing sycophantic answers to correct ones. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548
UNCONFIRMED: Anthropic’s newer percentages on reduced sycophancy (only secondary summaries seen; https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-personal-guidance exists, only opening fragment read). Do not quote numbers.
Mitigation (inference): ask for the strongest case against your idea; do not reveal your preferred answer in the prompt; ask it to check against data, not opinion.





Example: “how many n in banana?” correct answer 2 (b-a-n-a-n-a). Models may mis-state because they see tokens, not letters.
CONFIRMED (peer-reviewed/preprints, mixed): tokenization is a proposed cause: Cosma et al., “The Strawberry Problem”, EMNLP 2025, arXiv 2505.14172 (character-level info is weakly available inside tokens); Zhang et al., “Counting Ability of LLMs and Impact of Tokenization”, arXiv 2410.19730 (abstract: chain of thought can help and tokenization changes performance; abstract does not state that failures persist with CoT, but the full text, arxiv.org/html/2410.19730 read 2026-11-17, says significant failures remain even with CoT in models like GPT-4). https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14172 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19730
CONFIRMED counter-view: CharBench, arXiv 2508.02591, finds tokenization properties only weakly correlated with correctness; word length and true count matter more; Fu et al., arXiv 2412.18626, link errors to letter frequency and length. So say “tokenisation is a leading explanation, disputed in detail”, not settled. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02591
CONFIRMED fix evidence: arXiv 2410.14166 abstract does not state that Python code makes counting succeed (it says specialised math/coding LLMs still struggle and reasoning before answering is the most robust fix); the full text (arxiv.org/html/2410.14166, read 2026-11-17) says coding LLMs explicitly asked for Python complete the counting tasks, but fail in open-ended prompting. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14166 (authors Nan Xu and Xuezhe Ma, seen on the arXiv page 2026-11-17)
UNCONFIRMED: no Anthropic doc found that discusses letter counting or arithmetic limits. Only mechanism-level support: Anthropic documents a code execution tool and a bash tool that let Claude run code. Models overview lists server_tools.code_execution capability. P models/overview
Mitigation: have the agent run code (grep -o n | wc -l, seqkit stats, awk) and show the command and output; never trust a count it states in prose. Offer a live demo with count_tokens on a FASTA line (our own measurement is a valid source).





CONFIRMED official: “As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot.” P context-windows (already in fundamentals.md). Anthropic context-engineering article: finite “attention budget”.
CONFIRMED peer-reviewed: Liu et al., “Lost in the Middle”, arXiv 2307.03172 (TACL 2024 per my memory; the search did not confirm the venue): accuracy highest when relevant info is at the start or end of the input, lower in the middle, and falls as input grows. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172
Mitigation: curate inputs (head, counts, filtered tables), subagents, /clear, repeat key instructions in CLAUDE.md, not mid-chat.





CONFIRMED official: after auto-compaction “detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost”; put persistent rules in CLAUDE.md; long CLAUDE.md “reduce adherence”; CLAUDE.md is advisory, use a PreToolUse hook to block actions. C how-claude-code-works, C memory
Mitigation: short CLAUDE.md, hooks for must-never rules, /compact focus on ....





UNCONFIRMED (official): the fetched consistency page does not state that outputs vary or discuss temperature. It recommends explicit output formats, examples, retrieval grounding, prompt chaining; for guaranteed JSON use Structured Outputs. P increase-consistency
Practical (inference, plus doc-backed best-of-N idea above): the same prompt can give different answers; run twice and compare; record the exact command, model, version in your methods; do not treat an agent run as a reproducible analysis, the script it writes is.





CONFIRMED official proxy: “Allow Claude to say I don’t know” can drastically reduce false information, implying default answers lack calibrated hedging. P reduce-hallucinations. Claude Code docs: “Claude said it was done and it wasn’t quite, usually because it had no way to check its own work”; fix = “give Claude a check to run”. C best-practices
Mitigation: demand a verifying command (tests, row counts, md5, nextflow -stub) and read its output.





CONFIRMED official: Anthropic calls it “far from a solved problem”, “No browser agent is immune”; mitigations are RL training, classifiers on untrusted content, red teaming; improved safeguards cut internal attack success to about 1-2.4 percent in a Best-of-N test, still “meaningful risk”. https://www.anthropic.com/research/prompt-injection-defenses
CONFIRMED (Claude Code): permission prompts, network commands (curl, wget) not auto-approved, WebFetch summarised through a separate model call, sandboxed Bash (/sandbox), workspace trust dialog. Advice: review commands before approving, avoid piping untrusted content, use VMs for external services. “No system is completely immune.” C security
Relevance: a README, paper PDF, FASTA header, or web page the agent reads can contain instructions. Treat fetched content as data.





CONFIRMED: Sonnet 5.5 and the other current models list reliable knowledge cutoff and training data cutoff both Jun 2026 (reliable = where knowledge is most extensive; training cutoff = broader range of data). P models/overview
Consequence: newer tool versions (nf-core modules, Nextflow syntax, database releases) postdate it; check --version and the docs. Web search/fetch tools can fetch current info, with the injection caveat above.






Tasks: summarise text, draft prose, explain code or an error, convert formats (samplesheet CSV to JSON), write a script you can run. Shared property: you can inspect the output or run a test. (Inference.)
CONFIRMED peer-reviewed caveat: Maynez et al., “On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization”, ACL 2020: human raters found substantial hallucinated, unfaithful content in all neural summaries tested; pretrained models did better but not clean. Dated (pre-chat-LLM) evidence; direction still relevant. https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.173
UNCONFIRMED: an Anthropic-published faithfulness rate for current Claude summarising scientific papers. None found.
CONFIRMED mitigation (official): quote-first extraction and claim-by-claim citation checking. P reduce-hallucinations
Spot-check protocol (our advice): check every number, gene/sample name, direction of effect, and negation in the summary against the source; ask for quoted lines with page/section; omissions are harder to see, so skim the source’s abstract and limitations yourself.





Fetch Breunig’s author byline and his follow-up “How to Fix Your Context” (https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/26/how-to-fix-your-context.html, url unfetched) for named mitigations (quarantine, pruning).
Confirm TACL venue for Lost in the Middle; verify authors for 2410.14166 and 2410.19730 on arXiv.
Look for Anthropic text on temperature/non-determinism (API reference, not found here).
Measure our own banana/FASTA demos (count_tokens) and cite them as first-party.
