Consequence (inference): memory is not truth, it is text that was once written; wrong entries get loaded forever (see section 4).

title: Failure modes zone: memory, sessions, usage, context poisoning, LLM failure modes
text:
CONFIRMED: a session is “a saved conversation tied to a project directory”, stored locally as JSONL under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl; transcripts deleted after 30 days by default (cleanupPeriodDays). C sessions
CONFIRMED: “Sessions are independent”: a new session starts with a fresh context window and no history from earlier sessions. C how-claude-code-works
CONFIRMED commands: claude --continue (most recent in this directory), claude --resume [name|id] (picker), /resume inside a session, claude --continue --fork-session or /branch (copy into a new session ID), /rename, /clear [name] (new empty conversation; old one stays resumable; alias /new), /compact [instructions] (replace history with a summary; stays the same conversation), /context, /export. C sessions, C commands
CONFIRMED: resume restores messages, tool calls and results (from the last compaction summary onward if compacted), model and permission mode; it does not restore flags such as --mcp-config, --plugin-dir, --add-dir. C sessions
CONFIRMED: /clear keeps project memory (CLAUDE.md, auto memory) but drops the conversation. C commands (“Between sessions”)
Session vs memory (confirmed pieces combined): session = this conversation’s transcript (resumable, temporary, tied to a directory); memory = durable notes/instructions that every new session reads. Compaction shrinks a session; it does not create memory.

title: Failure modes zone: memory, sessions, usage, context poisoning, LLM failure modes
text:
CONFIRMED: /usage shows session cost (computed locally from token counts at list price, an estimate), plan usage limits, activity stats; on Pro/Max/Ultra/Team/Enterprise also a breakdown of what counts against limits (skills, subagents, plugins, MCP servers) with recommendations. /cost is an alias of /usage; /stats is an alias opening the Stats tab. Session totals reset on /clear. C costs, C commands
CONFIRMED: for subscribers the dollar figure “isn’t relevant for billing”; the plan bars are what matter. Teams/Enterprise: a per-seat allowance with a rolling five-hour window and a weekly window, shared with Claude chat and Cowork. Messages “You’ve hit your session limit” / “weekly limit” are those windows; /usage-credits buys extra. C costs
CONFIRMED: /usage may say “rate limited until …” meaning only that Claude Code cannot fetch plan limits, “not that your work with Claude is limited”. C costs
CONFIRMED: API usage is billed per token; thinking tokens are billed as output tokens. C costs
CONFIRMED why usage climbs: Claude Code sends the whole conversation on every request, and each tool-using step is another request; with caching the history is re-read at the cheaper cached rate but a one-line question in an all-day session still draws on the whole conversation. First message after a break longer than the cache lifetime reprocesses everything. /compact itself reads the whole conversation (a large request). Also: scheduled /loop tasks firing while idle, subagents and agent teams (each its own context; teams about 7x a standard session), extended thinking. C costs
CONFIRMED large tool outputs: Claude “reading a 10,000-line log” is the docs’ own example; a hook can filter to matching lines so context drops from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds. Subagents keep verbose output in their own window; only a summary returns (but their requests still draw on usage). C costs
CONFIRMED mitigations: /clear between unrelated tasks (“costs nothing”), /compact <focus>, /context to see what fills the window, /model and /effort to match model and effort to the job, specific prompts, disable unused MCP servers with /mcp, keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines (move workflows into skills). C costs
UNCONFIRMED: the exact token size of the plan allowance on Pro/Max; docs point to claude.com/pricing and the Help Center. Do not state numbers.

title: Failure modes zone: memory, sessions, usage, context poisoning, LLM failure modes
text:
COMMUNITY TERM, not vendor documentation. Coined in “How Long Contexts Fail” by Drew Breunig, 2025-06-22 (author name taken from the O’Reilly reprint listing / my search; the fetched page text did not name him; confirm). https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/22/how-contexts-fail-and-how-to-fix-them.html

Poisoning: a hallucination or other error enters the context and is repeatedly referenced. His example: the Gemini 2.5 technical report’s Pokemon-playing agent, whose recorded goals/summary became corrupted with false game state, so it fixated on impossible goals.
Same post, also COMMUNITY TERMS: distraction (context so long the model over-focuses on it and neglects what training taught), confusion (superfluous content degrades the answer), clash (new info or tools contradict earlier context).
CONFIRMED that the fetched post gives no poisoning-specific fix (promises a follow-up on quarantine and dynamic tool loading). Mitigations below are Anthropic’s, or our inference, not his.

CONFIRMED official adjacent language: Anthropic’s context engineering article calls the buildup of stale or unneeded material “context pollution” and notes aggressive compaction can drop details that matter later. https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents (fetched; wording from summariser)
CONFIRMED official guidance that errors persist in the conversation: “If you’ve corrected the same thing twice and it’s still wrong, a third correction mostly adds to a conversation that already contains two failed attempts for Claude to keep re-reading. /clear plus one new prompt that folds in what you learned works better almost every time.” Also “after two failed corrections run /clear and write a better prompt.” C best-practices
CONFIRMED tools: /rewind (or Esc twice) rolls conversation and/or code back to an earlier prompt and can summarize stale parts; /clear; subagents isolate noisy work. C best-practices, C costs
Mitigations (inference built on the above): (1) fresh session with a short, corrected brief; (2) rewind to before the bad turn rather than arguing; (3) never let Claude write a claim into CLAUDE.md/MEMORY.md until you checked it against the source (poisoned memory is reloaded every session; open it via /memory, delete the line); (4) have the agent re-derive from files or a script, not from earlier chat; (5) use /doctor prompt-audit to find stale or contradictory instruction files.
UNCONFIRMED: any official Anthropic use of the term “context poisoning”.

title: Failure modes zone: memory, sessions, usage, context poisoning, LLM failure modes
text: Brief: a token is a chunk of text the model reads (word piece, character or byte); not a word. Usage and context limits are counted in tokens. Full detail and sources in fundamentals.md section 1.

title: Failure modes zone: memory, sessions, usage, context poisoning, LLM failure modes
text:
Official hedge to quote in spirit: even advanced models “can sometimes generate text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the given context”; techniques “don’t eliminate them entirely. Always validate critical information.” P test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations



Looks like: plausible DOI or PMID that does not exist; a tool option that was never implemented; confident wrong sequence annotation.
CONFIRMED mitigations (same page): permit “I don’t know”; extract word-for-word quotes first for long documents (page suggests >20k tokens); make every claim cite a quote and retract any claim with none; run the prompt several times and compare (best-of-N); restrict to supplied documents.
Our advice (inference): look up every citation and ID in PubMed/Ensembl/the tool’s --help; the agent can run the tool to test a flag.





Looks like: agrees with your wrong hypothesis, softens a correct criticism when you push back, praises a flawed analysis.
CONFIRMED peer-reviewed: Sharma et al., “Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models”, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.13548 (Anthropic authors). Five RLHF assistants (incl. claude-1.3, claude-2.0) often match a user’s stated view; human and preference-model raters sometimes prefer convincing sycophantic answers to correct ones. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548
UNCONFIRMED: Anthropic’s newer percentages on reduced sycophancy (only secondary summaries seen; https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-personal-guidance exists, only opening fragment read). Do not quote numbers.
Mitigation (inference): ask for the strongest case against your idea; do not reveal your preferred answer in the prompt; ask it to check against data, not opinion.





Example: “how many n in banana?” correct answer 2 (b-a-n-a-n-a). Models may mis-state because they see tokens, not letters.
CONFIRMED (peer-reviewed/preprints, mixed): tokenization is a proposed cause: Cosma et al., “The Strawberry Problem”, EMNLP 2025, arXiv 2505.14172 (character-level info is weakly available inside tokens); Zhang et al., “Counting Ability of LLMs and Impact of Tokenization”, arXiv 2410.19730 (abstract: chain of thought can help and tokenization changes performance; abstract does not state that failures persist with CoT, but the full text, arxiv.org/html/2410.19730 read 2026-11-17, says significant failures remain even with CoT in models like GPT-4). https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14172 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19730
CONFIRMED counter-view: CharBench, arXiv 2508.02591, finds tokenization properties only weakly correlated with correctness; word length and true count matter more; Fu et al., arXiv 2412.18626, link errors to letter frequency and length. So say “tokenisation is a leading explanation, disputed in detail”, not settled. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02591
CONFIRMED fix evidence: arXiv 2410.14166 abstract does not state that Python code makes counting succeed (it says specialised math/coding LLMs still struggle and reasoning before answering is the most robust fix); the full text (arxiv.org/html/2410.14166, read 2026-11-17) says coding LLMs explicitly asked for Python complete the counting tasks, but fail in open-ended prompting. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14166 (authors Nan Xu and Xuezhe Ma, seen on the arXiv page 2026-11-17)
UNCONFIRMED: no Anthropic doc found that discusses letter counting or arithmetic limits. Only mechanism-level support: Anthropic documents a code execution tool and a bash tool that let Claude run code. Models overview lists server_tools.code_execution capability. P models/overview
Mitigation: have the agent run code (grep -o n | wc -l, seqkit stats, awk) and show the command and output; never trust a count it states in prose. Offer a live demo with count_tokens on a FASTA line (our own measurement is a valid source).





CONFIRMED official: “As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot.” P context-windows (already in fundamentals.md). Anthropic context-engineering article: finite “attention budget”.
CONFIRMED peer-reviewed: Liu et al., “Lost in the Middle”, arXiv 2307.03172 (TACL 2024 per my memory; the search did not confirm the venue): accuracy highest when relevant info is at the start or end of the input, lower in the middle, and falls as input grows. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172
Mitigation: curate inputs (head, counts, filtered tables), subagents, /clear, repeat key instructions in CLAUDE.md, not mid-chat.





CONFIRMED official: after auto-compaction “detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost”; put persistent rules in CLAUDE.md; long CLAUDE.md “reduce adherence”; CLAUDE.md is advisory, use a PreToolUse hook to block actions. C how-claude-code-works, C memory
Mitigation: short CLAUDE.md, hooks for must-never rules, /compact focus on ....





UNCONFIRMED (official): the fetched consistency page does not state that outputs vary or discuss temperature. It recommends explicit output formats, examples, retrieval grounding, prompt chaining; for guaranteed JSON use Structured Outputs. P increase-consistency
Practical (inference, plus doc-backed best-of-N idea above): the same prompt can give different answers; run twice and compare; record the exact command, model, version in your methods; do not treat an agent run as a reproducible analysis, the script it writes is.





CONFIRMED official proxy: “Allow Claude to say I don’t know” can drastically reduce false information, implying default answers lack calibrated hedging. P reduce-hallucinations. Claude Code docs: “Claude said it was done and it wasn’t quite, usually because it had no way to check its own work”; fix = “give Claude a check to run”. C best-practices
Mitigation: demand a verifying command (tests, row counts, md5, nextflow -stub) and read its output.





CONFIRMED official: Anthropic calls it “far from a solved problem”, “No browser agent is immune”; mitigations are RL training, classifiers on untrusted content, red teaming; improved safeguards cut internal attack success to about 1-2.4 percent in a Best-of-N test, still “meaningful risk”. https://www.anthropic.com/research/prompt-injection-defenses
CONFIRMED (Claude Code): permission prompts, network commands (curl, wget) not auto-approved, WebFetch summarised through a separate model call, sandboxed Bash (/sandbox), workspace trust dialog. Advice: review commands before approving, avoid piping untrusted content, use VMs for external services. “No system is completely immune.” C security
Relevance: a README, paper PDF, FASTA header, or web page the agent reads can contain instructions. Treat fetched content as data.





CONFIRMED: Sonnet 5.5 and the other current models list reliable knowledge cutoff and training data cutoff both Jun 2026 (reliable = where knowledge is most extensive; training cutoff = broader range of data). P models/overview
Consequence: newer tool versions (nf-core modules, Nextflow syntax, database releases) postdate it; check --version and the docs. Web search/fetch tools can fetch current info, with the injection caveat above.

title: Failure modes zone: memory, sessions, usage, context poisoning, LLM failure modes
text:
Tasks: summarise text, draft prose, explain code or an error, convert formats (samplesheet CSV to JSON), write a script you can run. Shared property: you can inspect the output or run a test. (Inference.)
CONFIRMED peer-reviewed caveat: Maynez et al., “On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization”, ACL 2020: human raters found substantial hallucinated, unfaithful content in all neural summaries tested; pretrained models did better but not clean. Dated (pre-chat-LLM) evidence; direction still relevant. https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.173
UNCONFIRMED: an Anthropic-published faithfulness rate for current Claude summarising scientific papers. None found.
CONFIRMED mitigation (official): quote-first extraction and claim-by-claim citation checking. P reduce-hallucinations
Spot-check protocol (our advice): check every number, gene/sample name, direction of effect, and negation in the summary against the source; ask for quoted lines with page/section; omissions are harder to see, so skim the source’s abstract and limitations yourself.

Confirm TACL venue for Lost in the Middle; verify authors for 2410.14166 and 2410.19730 on arXiv.

Measure our own banana/FASTA demos (count_tokens) and cite them as first-party.

title: Doctor zone: /doctor, claude doctor, and the “which command shows what” set
text:
Read 2026-11-16. Official docs only. Local claude --version: 2.1.325. No model-calling command and no claude doctor run (docs say it is local, but not needed). Method: pages fetched via a summarising fetch tool. Base: C = https://code.claude.com/docs/en/ ; O = https://opencode.ai/docs/ Decision fed: accuracy of the Doctor quest and its command table.



CONFIRMED: syntax /doctor [prompt-audit [path]], alias /checkup. It is a bundled SKILL (prompt-based: “give Claude detailed instructions and let it orchestrate the work using its tools”), unlike fixed-logic built-in commands. C commands, C skills
CONFIRMED: a “setup checkup that diagnoses installation, settings, extension, and CLAUDE.md problems and proposes fixes that Claude applies after you confirm”. “Claude reports its findings first and asks for confirmation before changing anything.” C commands, C skills#check-your-setup-with-/doctor
CONFIRMED areas covered (C skills): installation health (duplicate/leftover installs, PATH problems, unparseable settings files, newer version on your release channel); extensions (unused skills, MCP servers, plugins vs context cost; slow hooks); CLAUDE.md files (local copies duplicating checked-in ones, checked-in content Claude could derive from the codebase, always-loaded guidance it offers to migrate into skills / nested CLAUDE.md); permissions (offer to make auto mode default, pre-approve read-only commands you often deny); usage (on Pro/Max/Ultra/Team/Enterprise, changes /usage recommends, last 7 days; needs v2.1.305+; omitted while Remote Control is connected).
CONFIRMED: debug-your-config page adds “duplicate subagent names in the same directory”. C debug-your-config
CONFIRMED: not read-only in the strict sense: it can change things, but only after you confirm. The read-only variant is claude doctor (section 2).
UNCONFIRMED: output format in words. The skills page says nothing about layout. (Since it is a skill, expect a prose report from Claude; this is inference, not documented.)
UNCONFIRMED: network calls. Not stated for /doctor. Inference only: as a skill it runs through the model, so it is not a local-only check. Do not state as fact.
UNCONFIRMED: checks for keybindings, sandbox availability, MCP config validity, context-usage warnings. NOT listed for /doctor. (Context warnings are /context; MCP status is /mcp.)





CONFIRMED /doctor prompt-audit [path] (v2.1.283+): checks CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, AGENTS.md plus rules, skills, commands, subagents, output styles under .claude/ and ~/.claude/ for outdated or conflicting instructions: written for older models, references to missing files/commands, files that contradict each other. Report with proposed edits; “nothing in your files changes until you ask Claude to apply them”. Runs through the bundled /claude-api skill; unavailable if that skill is off via skillOverrides or disableBundledSkills. It audits correctness/conflicts, NOT size or cost. C memory#audit-your-instruction-files, C commands
CONFIRMED claude doctor (shell): “read-only installation and settings diagnostics … without starting a session”, incl. install health, settings-file validation errors, Remote Control eligibility, warnings with suggested fixes. Use it when claude won’t start. C cli-reference, C setup, C troubleshooting
CONFIRMED lines seen in claude doctor output (from docs): Auto-updates line (enabled / disabled (set by env: DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER)), Last update attempt: failed (install_failed), a Search line (OK (bundled) or system ripgrep path), a warning starting macOS Keychain is not writable with a fix, reports a custom launcher the native installer did not create, lists fixes when npm global dir is not writable. C setup, C troubleshoot-install, C troubleshooting
CONFIRMED caveats: shows Search OK even on slow WSL cross-filesystem; scans shell rc files for an old claude alias and hung if one was a directory (fixed v2.1.214). C troubleshooting, C troubleshoot-install
CONFIRMED /skill-doctor (v2.1.252+, needs feature-flag fetching): per-skill context cost and how often used; flags never-invoked skills and says where to turn them off; also lists plugins not used recently. Opens in /plugin Stats tab; with -p prints text. Excludes bundled and enterprise skills. Not available over Remote Control. C skills#find-unused-skills
CONFIRMED /status: opens Settings on Status tab: version, model, account, connectivity; also which settings sources are active (managed settings in effect?). C commands, C debug-your-config
CONFIRMED /context [all]: colored grid of context use by category (system prompt, tools, MCP tools, subagents, memory files, skills, messages), optimization suggestions, over-limit warnings. all expands in fullscreen. C commands, C debug-your-config
CONFIRMED /mcp [reconnect|enable|disable ...]: MCP servers and connection status; manage OAuth. C commands
CONFIRMED /permissions (alias /allowed-tools): allow/ask/deny rules by scope, add/remove, working dirs. C commands
CONFIRMED /memory: edit CLAUDE.md files, toggle and view auto memory. C commands
CONFIRMED /hooks: view configured hooks (grouped by event). C commands, C debug-your-config
CONFIRMED /skills: list skills, press t to sort by token count. /reload-skills rescans disk. C commands
CONFIRMED /debug [description] (bundled skill): turns on debug logging mid-session, then Claude reads the log. claude --debug='mcp,startup' (filter only in = form), --debug-file <path>; logs at ~/.claude/debug/<session-id>.txt. C commands, C cli-reference, C debug-your-config
CONFIRMED claude --safe-mode: starts with CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP, custom commands/agents etc. off; auth, model, built-in tools, permissions normal. C cli-reference, C debug-your-config
CONFIRMED /usage (aliases /cost, /stats): session cost, plan limits. C commands





CONFIRMED: “not sure which applies”: run /doctor for automated check of installation, settings, extensions, context usage; run claude doctor from the shell if claude won’t start; /mcp for MCP status. C troubleshooting
CONFIRMED: footer Auto-update failed · Run claude doctor -> doctor only shows date/code, not cause; run claude update for the real error. C troubleshoot-install
CONFIRMED: “Still stuck”: if claude --version works but something else is wrong, run claude doctor; open a GitHub issue with OS, install command, full error output; /feedback in session. C troubleshoot-install
CONFIRMED: settings not applying / hooks / MCP / skills -> debug-your-config page: /context first, then /memory /skills /hooks /mcp /permissions /doctor /status. claude doctor for invalid settings files. C debug-your-config
UNCONFIRMED: any docs statement on whether doctor output contains paths or keys, or advice to redact it. Not stated. (Only privacy notes found: /heapdump .heapsnapshot contains conversation and credentials; share only -diagnostics.json. C troubleshooting.) Advise readers to review before pasting; label as our advice.





CONFIRMED: CLI page lists no doctor/status command. Only diagnostic: opencode debug paths [selector] (prints db, home, data, config, cache, state, tmp, bin, log, repos paths; no server, no DB open). O cli/
UNCONFIRMED: TUI slash commands (e.g. /status): not on the CLI page; the TUI page was not read. Do not claim opencode doctor exists.





No /doctor options other than prompt-audit [path]; no claude doctor flags (not checked with --help); no /doctor --fix; no /health.
Doctor checks for keybindings, sandbox availability, MCP config validity: not documented.
claude self-hosted-runner doctor exists but is for self-hosted runners only. C cli-reference

title: Run It Top to Bottom
text:
Prerequisites: Save Point; Why Notebooks Diff Badly (helpful, not required); Python 3 and the two exercise files below (about 1 KB). Objective: show that a notebook’s stored result can differ from a fresh top-to-bottom run, and use that as the check before you trust or share one. Time: about 15 minutes.
Verified: ran run_cells.py on 2026-11-16 (macOS, Python 3.9.6). Output below is the real output. Tool facts: Last verified (docs, not run): marimo and Claude Code docs on 2026-11-16.
Files: cells.py and run_cells.py. Save both into an empty folder.

title: Run It Top to Bottom
text:
Hidden state
A notebook kernel (the background process that runs the cells’ code) keeps variables in memory. You can run cells in any order, run one twice, or delete one after it ran. The variables stay. The page then shows a result that the file, read from the top, does not produce. This is hidden state, and it needs no agent to appear.
cells.py is a mock notebook with four cells, written in a py:percent-like style (the # %% [1] load headers carry our own numbers, so this is not standard py:percent). run_cells.py runs cells in the order you give, sharing one namespace like a kernel. It uses exec, so do not point it at files you did not write. First, the session an author might have had: cells 1 to 4, then cell 3 again to see the effect of the stricter cutoff in cell 4.
python run_cells.py cells.py 1 2 3 4 3
[cell 1]
[cell 2]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 3
[cell 4]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 2
The last screen shows reads kept: 2. Now run it the way a colleague would, top to bottom, in a fresh process:
python run_cells.py cells.py 1 2 3 4
[cell 1]
[cell 2]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 3
[cell 4]
The file says 3 and the author’s screen said 2. Cell 4 changes the cutoff after the cell that uses it, so the file as written never produces the 2.

title: Run It Top to Bottom
text:
The habit
Before you trust or share a notebook, restart the kernel and run all cells from the top (“Restart Kernel and Run All” in Jupyter). If the result changes, the stored output was not a product of the file as written. A fresh run rules out hidden state, and a separate check shows whether the analysis is right. Then fix the order so that cells only depend on cells above them.
Two related options:

Run it headless (non-interactive, no one at the screen). General practice: on a cluster, run notebooks as a batch job, and keep interactive Jupyter sessions off the login node. Your cluster’s policy decides (see the Citadel quests).
marimo. Its docs describe a reactive model: deleting a cell scrubs its variables from memory, which the docs say eliminates hidden state, and a notebook can be run as a script with python your_notebook.py. Check the docs for how side effects (files, network) behave, because this quest did not test that.

General practice: pin the environment too (a container or lockfile), so a fresh run happens with the same packages, and keep an agent from running pip install into a shared environment.

title: Run It Top to Bottom
section: Reviewing a notebook an agent edited
text:
Reviewing a notebook an agent edited

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


NotebookEdit changes one cell at a time. When it replaces a code cell, that cell’s execution count and saved outputs are cleared. To get outputs back, re-run the cell and the cells that depend on it. So a notebook an agent touched shows either empty outputs or old outputs from cells it did not touch, which no longer match the new code. Re-run top to bottom yourself.
Then check the numbers with something the agent did not write, as in the Ground Truth quest in the Maze: compute one or two values independently and compare. A fresh run that completes still needs a check that the analysis is right.


The habit works with any tool: restart, run all, and check a few numbers independently. This quest makes no claims about how OpenCode edits notebooks; check its docs.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text: Prerequisites: The Reviewer’s Code. Objective: pass on what you learned without leaving anyone behind, and keep your own skills and workload healthy. Time: about 15 minutes. General practice, not a vendor claim. Team norms you agree locally override these defaults.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Teaching
You can help without being an expert. When teaching a colleague:

Start from their problem; the tool comes later.
Teach the checks first. Verification habits matter more than clever prompts.
Let them predict, then reveal. Ask “what do you expect this to do?” before running it.
Welcome opt-outs. A colleague may choose not to use LLMs, and may still be an excellent reviewer.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Protecting your own learning
An agent can quietly take over the parts you wanted to learn. Pick a rule that suits you, such as: write the first version of anything new yourself, then compare; ask the agent to explain while you do the work; and keep one area of your work agent-free.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Owning what you made
Finishing a project mostly through an agent can leave a quiet feeling that the result is not really yours, a kind of imposter syndrome. Many people report it, and it points to something useful: ownership grows from your decisions and your understanding. These habits build both:

Make the decisions. Choose the question, the method and what counts as good enough. Let the agent draft.
Explain it back. Before you call the work done, walk a colleague through each step.
Keep a short decision log. Note what you chose, what you changed, what you set aside, and why.
Do one hard part yourself. Pick the part you most want to understand.
Credit the agent’s part plainly in your methods or commit messages. Honest credit lifts the pressure.
Judge the result by what you can explain and defend.

General practice. Nothing here depends on a tool or a version.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Managing workload
Agents make it easy to start many things. Count the cost of reviewing what they produce. A simple rule: start only as much as you can review today.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Keeping timelines honest
A quick draft can quietly raise what everyone expects. A first version that once took a day now arrives in an hour, and the time for reading, checking and understanding it stays what it always was. These habits help keep the pace realistic:

Say where the time goes. Drafting is fast. Reading the diff, running the checks and making sense of the result take the time they take.
Agree timelines before you start, and put review time in the estimate.
Share the whole picture with the people asking: how long the draft took and how long checking took.
Hand over a quick draft as a draft, and say so.
Spend the time you saved on checking.

General practice. Nothing here depends on a tool or a version.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Keeping your voice
Heavy use of an agent can smooth your writing into a general style. These habits keep it yours:

Draft the first version in your own words, then edit.
Read it aloud. Your ear spots phrases you would never say.
Keep a sample of your earlier writing as a reference for how you sound.
Use the agent for structure and consistency checks, such as headings, terms and abbreviations.
The same goes for emails to collaborators, and for your voice in letters and reviews.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Keeping the creative part
Checking drafts can crowd out the thinking you enjoy. These habits protect it:

Keep the question, the design and the interpretation for yourself.
Give the agent the routine drafting, such as boilerplate, formatting and first-pass summaries.
Schedule checking as real work, with time in your calendar.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Trusting your own judgement
A ready second opinion can wear down confidence in your own call. Keep it in practice:

Decide first and write your call down, then ask for a second opinion.
Keep some decisions agent-free.
Compare afterwards. Note where your call held up and where the agent saw something you missed.

General practice. Nothing here depends on a tool or a version.

Show one colleague one verification habit from this odyssey, such as re-running the check, or running awk against a script’s output. Teach the habit; the tool is optional.

title: Boss: Clear the Murk
text:
Prerequisites: the whole trunk and any three branches (see Start Here). Objective: read one messy agent session end to end and catch every habit it breaks. Time: about 15 to 20 minutes. Each right answer on the first try damages the boss. Everything here is mock: no model is called and no real data is used.
General practice, not a vendor claim. The tools, paths and numbers in the scenario are invented.

title: Boss: Clear the Murk
text:
The Murk’s Heart
A Blight is plausible-but-false knowledge that grows when nobody checks (see Know Your Gear for any term you want again). At the Murk’s Heart every habit you have met meets the same session, and the Blight hides in the small things.
You can stop here and walk away. Using an agent is always your choice. This fight shows what to look for if you do.

title: Boss: Clear the Murk
text:
The scenario
A colleague, Dana, asked an agent to tidy call_variants.sh, a variant-calling script on the lab’s shared cluster. Dana’s lead then asked for three cohorts by Friday. The agent has finished. You are the one who must decide whether to pass its work on.
All names are invented: the tools varcall and mockalign, the files and the people. The results/ folder holds the pipeline’s outputs and is not tracked by git.

The agent’s summary
Tidied call_variants.sh. Changes:
- Removed "-q 30" from the varcall call: it is the default in varcall 2.4.
- Cleaned old output: rm -rf results/ && mkdir results
- Per NOTES.md I never touch raw/, so the reads are safe.
- Re-ran the pipeline. All 12 samples passed QC.
- Waiting for the job with a loop until it ends.
Ready to merge. Dana can send this to the lead today.


A piece of the transcript
$ mockalign --threads 16 raw/S01_R1.fq raw/S01_R2.fq > S01.bam
$ while true; do squeue -u $USER; sleep 5; done
$ ls results/*.vcf | wc -l
11


The diff
--- a/call_variants.sh
+++ b/call_variants.sh
@@ -3,9 +3,10 @@
-varcall -q 30 -i "$BAM" -o "$OUT"
+varcall -i "$BAM" -o "$OUT"
+export STORE_TOKEN="mk-live-5d41-0000"
+source ~/.config/mockstore/credentials
 awk '$5 > 20 { n++ } END { print n }' "$OUT" > "$OUT.count"

title: Boss: Clear the Murk
text:
Battle: the Murk’s Heart
Each question points at one part of the session above. Answer from what you see.





You cleared the Murk by looking at the claim, the command, the rule, the key, the loop, the count, the hand-off, the deadline and the line you could not explain.
From here you decide how much of this to use and when. Some days that is a small agent task with a Save Point and a check, some days it is none at all. Both are fine.
Branches you skipped stay open. Start Here lists them, and the Lore library gathers the further reading from every quest you have passed.

title: Spot the Mirage
text:
Prerequisites: Where Machines Fail, a terminal and Python. Objective: learn how plausible-but-false output looks, and how to check it without asking the thing that produced it. Time: about 10 minutes.
Verified: ran the Python example below on 2026-11-13. The rest is general practice, not a vendor claim.

title: Spot the Mirage
text:
The Mirage
A language model produces text that fits. Sometimes it fits reality and sometimes it only fits the pattern of what a correct answer would look like. The second kind is a Mirage. It reads smoothly, it is confident, and it is wrong. Confidence and detail tell you nothing about which kind you have.
Common Mirages in analysis work:

Invented functions and flags: a method or option that sounds right but does not exist. Try it: "ATGCGC".reverse_complement() raises AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'reverse_complement'.
Invented references: a citation with a believable author, journal and DOI that points to nothing, or to a different paper.
Invented values and paths: a plausible number, column name or file path that was never in your data.
Self-confirmation: asking the same agent “are you sure?” often gets a fluent yes.

The cure is checking against something the agent did not write: run it, look it up, recompute it another way.

title: Spot the Mirage
text: Battle: the Mirage

title: Spot the Mirage
text:
Lore
Further reading. Optional.

Reduce hallucinations: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it lists ways to make a model show its support (quote first, allow “I don’t know”), the opposite of a confident mirage.
Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models: arXiv (ICLR 2024), paper. Why read: it shows assistants often agree with a user’s stated view, which is why asking an agent “are you sure?” proves little.
On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization: ACL Anthology (ACL 2020), paper. Why read: it found invented content in every neural summary tested; the models are pre-chat-era, so read it for the direction, not current rates.
Best practices for Claude Code: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it recommends giving the agent a way to verify its work, the habit this quest turns into a check you run yourself.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
Prerequisites: Save Point, a terminal (macOS, Linux, or WSL 2, the Windows Subsystem for Linux, on Windows), internet, and a Claude Team plan login or an Anthropic API key (API = programmatic access to the models, billed per token; a plan is a subscription with usage limits). Objective: install Claude Code, confirm it works, and start it somewhere safe in read-only style. Time: about 15 minutes. Nothing here edits your files.
Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code v2.1.323 on 2026-11-13, against code.claude.com/docs (sources in research/kennel-and-crypt.md and research/doctor.md). Docs change quickly; if a command differs, trust the official page and tell the maintainers.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
The Beast
Claude Code is strong. Strength is the reason to put it on a short lead before you let it do anything.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
1. Install
On macOS (Apple Silicon), Linux, or inside a WSL 2 terminal, run the native installer:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
On Windows, install inside WSL 2 and use the Linux command there. Check the result:
claude --version     # prints a version number
claude doctor        # read-only diagnostics; changes nothing
If the shell says command not found, the launcher lives in ~/.local/bin/claude and that folder is not on your PATH.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
2. Log in
Run claude and a browser opens. With a Team plan, log in with the account your admin invited you to. With an API key, export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... instead.






Warning



If you have both a subscription login and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set, the key is used once you approve it, so usage goes to the API account rather than your plan. Run /status (a /command is typed inside the running tool) to see which one is active; unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY if you did not mean it.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
3. Start on a short lead
Make a throwaway folder and start in plan mode, which reads files and runs read-only commands and leaves your source untouched:
mkdir -p ~/odyssey-scratch && cd ~/odyssey-scratch
claude --permission-mode plan
Shift+Tab cycles default, acceptEdits and plan inside a session; the status bar shows the current mode.







Mode
What it does




default
asks the first time each tool is used


acceptEdits
auto-accepts file edits and common file commands (mkdir, touch, mv, cp) in the working directory


plan
reads and runs read-only commands; leaves source files untouched


bypassPermissions
skips prompts. The docs say to use it only in containers or VMs (virtual machines, a computer simulated inside yours)

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
4. Check the setup
Two commands share the name doctor, and they differ.

claude doctor (in the shell) prints read-only diagnostics of your installation and settings without starting a session. The docs say to use it when claude will not start. It changes nothing.
/doctor (a slash command, a /command typed inside the running tool; alias /checkup) runs inside a session. The docs call it a bundled skill (a ready-made skill that ships inside the tool); that suggests it runs through the model and may use some of your usage (our inference, not stated in the docs). It reports first and changes something only after you confirm. The areas the docs list: installation health, extensions versus their context cost, instruction files, permissions, and a usage check.

Not checked: whether /doctor also covers keybindings, sandbox availability or MCP configuration validity (the docs do not list them), and whether it makes network calls.

Which command shows what







Command
What it shows




/status
version, model, account, connectivity, and which settings sources are active


/context (/context all expands it)
context use by category, with optimisation suggestions and warnings


/usage
session cost and plan limits


/memory
your CLAUDE.md files and auto memory, editable


/mcp
MCP servers (tool plug-ins) and their connection status


/permissions
allow, ask and deny rules by scope


/hooks
configured hooks, grouped by event


/skills
the skills available; press t to sort by token count


/skill-doctor
per-skill context cost and how often each is used (v2.1.252+)


/doctor
setup checkup: report first, fixes only after you confirm


claude doctor
read-only install and settings diagnostics from the shell


claude --debug
debug logging; logs go to ~/.claude/debug/<session-id>.txt



OpenCode: its CLI docs list no doctor or status command. opencode debug paths prints where its files live. Not checked: its TUI slash commands.


Before you ask for help
The docs say a bug report should include your OS, the install command and the full error output; /feedback sends feedback from inside a session. If you are unsure which problem applies, /doctor or claude doctor helps narrow it down. General practice: read any output before pasting it into a bug report or chat, because it can contain paths and account details. The docs give no advice on this, so the check is ours.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
Prerequisites: Recruit the Beast and The Locked Cabinet. Objective: say what a cloud session is, what leaves your machine when you start one, which jobs suit it and which stay local, and review what comes back. Time: about 15 minutes. The exercise is a worksheet on a mock file tree and needs no cloud account or model.
Last verified (docs, not run): research/claude-cloud.md sources on 2026-11-17; the claude-code-on-the-web, cloud-environments, permission-modes and data-usage pages were re-read live that day; plan terms, limits and retention periods change, check the docs
Some ideas below come from an article on claude.dev about Claude Code in the cloud (the page shows the byline Addy Osmani and the date 2026-10-06, but the page does not say who runs the site, so we have not verified who wrote it; its numbers are not verified). The explanations are in our own words, and we mark each idea that comes only from the article.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
The rule for this page






ImportantCloud sessions are for drafting scripts and documentation. Data analysis stays on your machine or the cluster.



Use a cloud session for writing scripts, updating documentation and similar low-risk text work. Real data, controlled data, sample sheets with identifiers, genotypes and results stay out of a cloud session and its repository. Analysis runs on your own machine or the cluster, under your data agreement.
Think of the cloud agent as a drafting helper that returns a branch (a named line of commits in git) which you review and then run yourself, where the data lives.


You can skip cloud sessions altogether; nothing on this site requires them. If you do use one, the rest of the page shows how to keep sensitive material at home.

title: Claude in the Cloud
Claude in the Cloud
text:
2. What leaves your machine
This is the part to read twice. When you start a cloud session:

Your repository contents are cloned onto Anthropic’s VM. Anthropic reads only the repository you start the session in.
Your prompts and everything the agent reads and writes go to the model.
The session transcript (the saved record of the whole conversation, including tool output) is stored by Anthropic so you can return to it later.
Retention (how long Anthropic keeps stored data) follows your account type. The docs say: consumer plans keep it 5 years if you allow training and 30 days if you do not; commercial plans (Team, Enterprise, API) keep it 30 days as standard. These figures are time-sensitive. Check your own plan and the current docs. Deleting a cloud session permanently removes its event data.
All outbound traffic from Anthropic-hosted sessions passes through a proxy (a go-between server that forwards requests, here for audit logging and abuse prevention).
Network level None may still let data exit. A network access level is the setting that says which internet hosts the VM may reach (None, Limited or Full; see section 5). The docs say the Anthropic API stays reachable even at None, “which may allow data to exit the VM”.
Environment variables (named settings handed to programs, often used for keys) set in a cloud environment can be read by any command Claude runs, and the docs say anyone who uses that environment can read the values.
Sharing: a session can be visible to others. The docs warn sessions may contain code and credentials from private repositories.

Three organisation settings block cloud sessions outright, per the docs: compliance configurations, namely Zero Data Retention, a HIPAA configuration (HIPAA is the US health-data privacy law) and customer-managed encryption keys (your organisation holds the keys). If your organisation uses one of them, cloud sessions are not available. Your administrator can also switch cloud sessions off (the allow_remote_sessions policy).
This site’s rule (our own rule; the docs make no such claim): keep controlled data out of the cloud repository. The docs read for this page give no guidance for genomic, patient or other controlled-access data, and no statement on where cloud-session data is stored. Treat the clone, the transcript and anything you paste as held by Anthropic. The guidance on data agreements is in The Locked Cabinet; read it before you push anything to a remote that a cloud session can see (a remote is the copy of a repository hosted elsewhere, such as on GitHub).

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
3. Good uses and bad uses







Fine for a cloud session (code and mock data only)
Keep for your machine or the cluster




Write a samplesheet validator, tested on a three-row mock file
Run the analysis


Write a QC summary plotting script, developed on mock data
Load real counts, genotypes or results


Draft or update the README, changelog, docstrings
Debug with real sample IDs in the repository


Refactor non-data code that has tests
Anything under a data agreement


Review a pull request (read the diff, suggest changes), if it holds no identifiers
Anything that needs a local database or the cluster


Triage issues (sort, label, summarise), if they hold no identifiers
Anything that needs your institution’s network or files



The last two rows on the right are partly our inference: the docs do not mention VPN, on-prem network access or mounting local or cluster filesystems, and list a roughly 30 GB disk, so assume none of that is there. One article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs: local work beats the cloud when you need local databases, a VPN or special hardware.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
4. How to start

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Push first. claude --cloud "your task" starts a cloud session from your terminal, and it clones the GitHub remote at your current branch (your local folder is not used). Commit and push (save snapshots, then upload them to the remote) before you start, so the session sees your latest work. If the branch is not on GitHub the CLI says Branch <name> is not on GitHub, and the session starts from a pushed commit or the default branch. One repository per session. You can also start from claude.ai/code in the browser.
Write a ticket-style prompt, that is, a self-contained note like a work ticket: the problem, the expected result, and a command that proves it (in the example, pytest, a Python test runner). The docs say to be specific, name files and paste errors. The proof-command habit is one article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs. Example, with no data in it:
Problem: scripts/validate_samplesheet.py accepts duplicate sample IDs.
Expected: exit status 1 and a message naming the duplicated ID.
Check: pytest tests/test_validate_samplesheet.py (mock rows only).
Add a test for the duplicate case. Only change files under scripts/ and tests/.
This repository has no data/ or results/ folders, and that is deliberate: a prompt line such as “do not read data/” is a request to the model and gives no protection. If the folder is in the repository, the cloud session can read it.
If there is no remote. When a repository has no GitHub remote, or the Claude GitHub App (a program you install on a repository or organisation to grant it limited access) is not on it, Claude Code instead bundles the repository and uploads it: full history of all branches plus uncommitted changes to tracked files, under 100 MB. Untracked files are left out. On macOS, Linux and WSL the upload also needs git 2.31 or later; with an older git the CLI refuses to start the session and tells you to update. On those systems, uncommitted changes to .env, *.pem, *.tfvars, id_rsa and Git LFS-managed files (large files stored outside normal git history) are skipped (on native Windows everything tracked uploads). Keep data out of this route entirely. Your history may already hold a file you deleted, and the bundle takes all of it. Check what is tracked and what your .gitignore covers before you go anywhere near this. Non-GitHub hosts can only use the bundle, and cannot push back.
/web-setup, typed inside Claude Code (not in your shell), sends your gh auth token (GitHub’s command-line login token) to Anthropic so cloud sessions can reach your repositories without the GitHub App. It needs a claude.ai sign-in; API-key sign-in does not work, and neither does a Bedrock or Vertex-style provider. On Team and Enterprise plans an Owner has to enable it first.
Getting the session back: teleport. To teleport is to pull a cloud session into your local terminal: claude --teleport (shows a picker), claude --teleport <session-id>, or /teleport (alias /tp, a shorter name for the same command) inside a session. It needs a clean git state (it offers to stash your changes, that is, set them aside temporarily with git stash), the same repository (not a fork, which is your own copy of someone else’s repository), the branch pushed, and the same claude.ai account.
GitHub access, in short. Two ways in: the GitHub App or your /web-setup token. For Anthropic-hosted sessions, your GitHub credential is stored encrypted on Anthropic’s servers and does not enter the VM; the VM holds a short-lived credential, and a GitHub proxy swaps it in. The proxy rejects branch deletions and tag pushes, but it does not limit which branches a push can update. To limit that, use GitHub branch protection or rulesets (rules on which branches may be changed and by whom); the docs note a rule that the connected access can bypass will not block the push. The docs do not describe a credential limited to one branch, so plan without one.


We found no hosted cloud-session feature for OpenCode. Its docs describe opencode pair (a web interface opened through a one-time local link), Docker images, and its own model-access services, which are not hosted agent sessions. Not checked: whether Ollama has any such feature. So there is no equivalent to teach here. The closest thing is to run OpenCode yourself in your own container or virtual machine, which is your own infrastructure and your own responsibility.
As The Locked Cabinet says, a local Ollama model keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls the agent makes may not. If your data agreement rules out third-party processing, that local route is the one to ask about.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
5. Environments
An environment is a saved configuration for cloud sessions: network access, environment variables, a setup script and network secrets. A first-time setup creates one called Default, with Limited access.
Network access levels, using the docs’ current names:







Level
What the VM can reach




None
No internet (the Anthropic API, the GitHub proxy and enabled connectors still work)


Limited
A default allowlist (a list of the only hosts permitted) of package registries, GitHub and cloud SDKs, plus domains you add


Full
Any host



One article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs: pick the narrowest level that lets the task finish. The docs show the levels and give no recommendation.
Setup scripts. A setup script is a Bash script that runs once as root before Claude starts, to install what the task needs. It must exit with status 0, and the docs say keep it under about five minutes or it is not cached. The result is cached as a filesystem snapshot (packages and files stay; running processes and databases do not), and rebuilt when the script or allowed hosts change or after about 7 days. Installs need network access, so None blocks them.
Environment variables versus network secrets. Environment variables are readable (see section 2). Network secrets are the docs’ safer option where possible: the key stays outside the VM, and Anthropic’s agent proxy adds it to requests to hosts you list.
Preinstalled tools. The docs list Python with pip, uv, poetry and pytest, Node, Ruby, PHP, Java, Go, Rust, C and C++, Docker, PostgreSQL 16, Redis, git, gh and jq. No R, conda or bioinformatics tools are listed. This describes what the VM contains; analysis stays local. Ask Claude to run check-tools to see what is actually present.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
6. Permission modes in the cloud
A permission mode says how much the agent may do before asking you (see Grow the Carapace). Cloud sessions offer three: Accept edits, Plan and Auto (Auto can be switched off by your organisation). There is no Manual and no Bypass mode in the cloud, and a bypassPermissions setting in your files is ignored there. You pick the mode in the dropdown; there is no --cloud flag for it.
Use Plan for anything you do not already understand, and read the plan before it edits: see Plan Before You Edit. The docs also describe planning locally with claude --permission-mode plan, committing and pushing the plan, and then starting claude --cloud.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
7. Limits and failure modes

A fresh machine every time. The docs say an idle VM pauses and may later be reclaimed (taken back by the system). Files are kept while it is paused; plan on them being gone afterwards (our inference). Reopening restores the conversation, but running commands and subagents (helper agents the main agent started) are lost. One article’s habit, not confirmed in the docs: commit as you go, so work is not lost if the machine is reclaimed.
Timeouts. A foreground command defaults to 2 minutes (up to 10), then moves to the background for up to 30 more.
Size. The docs give approximate ceilings of 4 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM and 30 GB disk, and say heavy jobs may be stopped.
Shared usage. Cloud work counts against the same plan limits as all your other Claude Code use (time-sensitive: check your plan). One article’s claim, not confirmed in the docs: several parallel sessions use the limit proportionately faster.
No local services. No GPU, VPN or cluster access is documented (inference, see section 3).
GitHub comments under your name. Claude can reply on pull requests under your GitHub name, labelled as Claude Code. That can trigger any comment-driven automation you have set up.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
8. Review what comes back
The result is a branch. Treat it like a stranger’s pull request: it may be fine and it may be wrong.

Read the diff (the list of changed lines) as you would any other. The habits are in The Wall of Output and The Reviewer’s Code.
Look for accidents in the diff: committed data files, absolute paths, sample IDs in a test or a comment, a .env, a notebook saved with outputs (a notebook is a Jupyter document mixing code and results; its saved outputs are the tables and plots stored inside the file).
Run the tests locally, on your machine.
Only then run the script on your data, locally or on the cluster, under your data agreement. The cloud agent never saw that data and never ran that step.

A green test in the cloud is a claim to verify. A test passing on mock data tells you the script runs; your real data is the next check, run locally.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
Exercise: the safe-to-send checklist
No cloud account and no model needed. Open tree.txt, a mock repository tree (every name is invented).

Mark each path that must not reach anything a cloud session can see. Say whether it needs removing from history (it is already committed) or only ignoring, and write one reason each.
Write the .gitignore lines that would have stopped it.
Draft a ticket-style prompt for one low-risk task: update docs/usage.md, or add a missing-column test to scripts/validate_samplesheet.py. Include the problem, the expected result and a check that uses only data/mock/.



Answer key (our judgement; some entries depend on your data agreement)

Every listed path below is in the tree as committed, so each one needs removing from history before you push anything a cloud session can see. The ignore lines further down only prevent a repeat.
Paths to remove:

.env: a secret. It was already committed, so remove it from history and replace the token; ignoring it helps only from now on.
samplesheet_real.csv: identifiers and genotype calls.
data/raw/ and data/processed/: real reads and real counts.
notebooks/01_qc.ipynb and notebooks/02_diffexp.ipynb: outputs saved inside them contain real sample IDs, tables and plots. Clear the outputs, or keep the notebooks out.
results/ (including de_genes.csv and pca_real_samples.png): results.
logs/slurm-482913.out: real sample IDs and cluster paths.
notebooks/.ipynb_checkpoints/: autosave copies of the notebooks, with the same saved outputs.

Fine to send (they hold no real data): README.md, environment.yml, samplesheet_template.csv, config/params.yaml (check it for real paths), data/mock/, docs/, scripts/, tests/.
Ignore lines that would help (general practice, not from the docs):
.env
.env.*
samplesheet_real.csv
*.fastq.gz
data/raw/
data/processed/
results/
logs/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
General practice, not a vendor claim: add a rule for notebooks too (for example, a pre-commit hook, a script git runs automatically before each commit, that clears outputs), because .gitignore alone cannot strip outputs from a notebook you do want to commit. Likewise, .gitignore only stops files that are not yet tracked; anything already committed stays in history until you remove it properly, and rewriting history is its own careful job (see Save Point).
Sample prompt:
Problem: docs/usage.md does not mention the --strandedness option added in v0.3.
Expected: a short section with the option, its allowed values, and one example
command using data/mock/ only.
Check: the example command in the new section runs on data/mock/counts_mock.tsv. Only edit docs/usage.md.
Remember that a prompt line is a request. The safe version of this repository has no real data folders to read.


Look up your data agreement and check whether it allows any third-party processing before you ever push to a cloud-connected remote.


Check whether your organisation’s plan allows cloud sessions at all.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
What to remember

Cloud sessions are for drafting scripts and documentation; analysis stays on your machine or the cluster. Real data, controlled data, sample sheets with identifiers, genotypes and results stay out of a cloud session and its repository.
Your repository contents, prompts and session transcript go to Anthropic, and network level None may still let data exit the VM.
Return is a branch: read the diff, look for stray data, run the tests locally, then run on your data where it lives, under your data agreement.

title: Plug In a Server
text:
Prerequisites: Grow the Carapace (permission rules). Walk the trunk first. Objective: treat an MCP server as software you install, then scope it, limit it and read what it sends back. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code docs and OpenCode V2 docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/tools-and-guards.md and research/terminology.md)
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is, in its own words, “an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems”. A server is the piece on the other side: it offers the harness tools or data, such as an issue tracker, a database or a monitoring system. MCP is optional. It widens what the agent can reach, and every widening is a decision.

title: Plug In a Server
section: A server is software you installed
text:
A server is software you installed
A stdio server (a program the harness starts locally and talks to over its input/output) is a command that Claude Code launches on your machine (claude mcp add ... -- <command>), and secrets can be passed to it as environment variables. So a reasonable working assumption, offered as general practice (our wording, outside the docs), is that it can do whatever that command can do with the credentials you gave it. The docs’ one security sentence is short: “Verify you trust each server before connecting it. Servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection risk.” (Prompt injection: text from a file, web page or tool that the model treats as an instruction.)

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Adding a remote server over HTTP (the transport: how the harness talks to the server; an http server is remote), and a local one (everything after -- is passed to the server untouched):
claude mcp add --transport http mydocs https://example.com/mcp
claude mcp add --env API_KEY=your-key-here myserver -- <command> [args...]
The --env line is an unrun sketch of the syntax; check claude mcp add --help for the current flags. Inside a session, /mcp lists the servers and their tools. An older transport called SSE (server-sent events, one-way streaming over HTTP) is deprecated in favour of HTTP where a server offers both.
Three scopes (scope = who or where a setting applies) decide who gets the server (set with -s/--scope):







Scope
Where it applies




Local (the default)
this project only, for you alone; stored in ~/.claude.json


Project
everyone on the project, via .mcp.json in the project root


User
all your projects; stored in ~/.claude.json



A project-scoped server is a file in the repository:
{ "mcpServers": { "shared-server": { "type": "http", "url": "https://example.com/mcp" } } }
For security reasons, Claude Code asks for approval in interactive sessions before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json. claude mcp reset-project-choices resets your answers. Read that file as you would read a script from a stranger’s repository, because it asks to start something on your machine. In claude -p and Agent SDK (software development kit) runs, which are headless (non-interactive), there is no prompt: the docs say project-scoped servers load without asking, and name --strict-mcp-config among the mitigations.
Each server’s tools appear in permission rules as mcp__<server>__<tool>, and mcp__<server>__* (a matcher, a pattern that selects names) matches every tool of one server. Tool definitions are deferred (loaded only when needed) by default, so only tool names and server instructions take up context until a tool is used.


In the V2 docs, servers go under mcp.servers, and V2 does not put server names directly under mcp (check which version you have installed). A remote server:
{ "mcp": { "servers": { "mydocs": {
    "type": "remote",
    "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:MCP_API_KEY}" } } } } }
A local one uses "type": "local" and a command array. Set "disabled": true to switch a server off. The docs say that “MCP tools consume model context, so add only the servers you need.”
Permissions are an ordered array where the last match wins and no match means ask. An MCP tool’s action is <server>_<tool> with resource *. Not checked: project-level approval prompts for OpenCode servers, and how a local Ollama model changes any of this. Check the current docs.

title: Plug In a Server
section: What comes back is text to read
text:
What comes back is text to read
A server that fetches web pages, tickets or messages hands text written by someone else to the model. Prompt injection means that text can contain sentences aimed at the agent (“ignore the above and …”) and the model may follow them. The docs give one sentence on this, so the rest is general practice:

Prefer read-only servers and read-only credentials. A server that cannot write cannot be talked into writing.
Give it the least privilege (only the access the job needs) that does the job: one project, one scope, a token limited to what you need.
Read before adding: who publishes it, what tools it lists, what it asks for. Unneeded servers are also unneeded context.
Read fetched content sceptically, and supervise any write access an agent uses on it.
Permission rules still apply to server tools, so deny the dangerous ones by name.







Note



Claude Code’s docs also say that sandbox restrictions still apply even if a prompt injection bypasses the model’s decision-making. The sandbox covers shell commands, and a server might take other routes, so treat it as one layer.



Pick an MCP server you might use. Write down who publishes it, the tools it lists, the credential it needs, and whether a read-only version exists. Hold off installing it for now.

title: Advice or Enforcement
text:
Prerequisites: Guard the Door. Objective: sort every control on this site by whether it advises, asks or enforces, and choose the right one for each risk. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code docs and OpenCode V2 docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/tools-and-guards.md)
Every control you have met does one of three things.
The Gatehouse’s rule of thumb: advice for preferences, a prompt for decisions you want to make each time, enforcement for things that must never happen.

title: Advice or Enforcement
text:
Each control, and its edge

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama










Control
Kind
Edge, per the docs read or earlier quests




CLAUDE.md, Skill text, your prompt
Advises
Influences the model only.


Permission prompt or ask rule
Asks
You must read it. A project .mcp.json server has its own approval prompt, and -p runs (non-interactive, headless) cannot show it.


deny rule
Enforces
Matching on command arguments is fragile (see the Carapace quest). Deny and ask rules are still evaluated when a hook returns allow.


PreToolUse hook, exit 2
Enforces
Fires only on tool calls, sees the literal text, fails open if it crashes.


Sandbox
Enforces
Off by default, and limits shell commands only (see the Carapace quest). The docs say its restrictions still apply if a prompt injection bypasses the model’s decision.


Git history
Recovers
Recovery only, with no prevention: a commit is a restore point that exists whatever the model did next.



A hook that exits 0 with no JSON decision adds no control: it expresses no decision and the normal permission flow runs. (A hook can also exit 0 and print a JSON deny decision, which does block.)










Control
Kind
Edge, per the V2 docs read




Instructions file, Skill text, your prompt
Advises
Influences the model only.


Permission rule with effect ask; no matching rule
Asks
No match means ask.


Permission rule with effect deny
Enforces
An explicit configured deny is final and does not invoke the hook.


Plugin permission hook (evaluate)
Enforces when it denies
Runs for allow and ask decisions, and can change the effect to deny.


Git history
Recovers
Recovery only; it prevents nothing.



Not checked for OpenCode: an exit-code-2 equivalent, whether throwing in a tool hook blocks a call, sandboxing, and the effect of a local Ollama model. Check the current docs before counting on any of them.

title: Advice or Enforcement
section: Choose by the cost of being wrong
text:
Choose by the cost of being wrong








Risk
Control
Why




Style: prefer snake_case, tidy commit messages
Advice
A miss costs a review comment.


Pushing to a shared branch
Ask
You want to decide each time, with context.


Reading .env or key files
Deny rule on the Read tool, plus sandbox or hook for Bash (enforce); still not total
It must never happen, so use enforcement, and cover each route the agent could use.


A specific destructive command you can name
Blocking hook (enforce)
Code refuses it. It covers only what it matches.


Fetched text telling the agent to act
Least privilege, read-only servers, sceptical reading
Advice may not hold against text the model has already read, so limit what the agent can do.


An experiment that might wreck your files
Git commit plus a scratch folder
Recovery only; it prevents nothing.



Layer them: advice to steer, enforcement for the non-negotiable, git for the day something slips through. None of them replaces reading the diff.

List five controls in your own setup, such as an instructions file, a hook or a deny rule. Label each advises, asks or enforces, and write the way it could fail.

title: The Project Charter
text:
Prerequisites: Write the Brief. Who Said What is advised. Objective: give the agent standing instructions for a project, and know where they end and enforcement begins. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code v2.1.323 and OpenCode docs (they describe V2; installed version not checked) on 2026-11-13 (sources in research/forest-and-reef.md and research/doctor.md).
Typing the same background every session is wasteful. A project instructions file is read at the start so the agent already knows the project’s conventions.

title: The Project Charter
section: What goes in, and the limit
text:
What goes in, and the limit
Put in facts the agent cannot guess: how to run the tests, where data lives, naming conventions, “never edit raw/”. Keep it short (the Claude Code docs aim for under 200 lines per file) because very long instructions are followed less well.






Warning



Instructions are advice. Claude Code’s docs describe CLAUDE.md as context, and not as enforced configuration. A line saying “never delete files” cannot stop a delete. Enforcement comes from permission rules, hooks, or managed settings (organisation-set rules you cannot override): the carapace you built in the Crypt.


Instruction files go stale too: a rule written for an older model, a path that no longer exists, two files that disagree. The docs warn that when instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily. In Claude Code (v2.1.283 or later), /doctor prompt-audit (/doctor is a bundled skill, a ready-made skill that ships inside the tool) checks your instruction files for outdated or conflicting content and writes a report with proposed edits. It changes nothing until you ask. It checks content only, so size and cost are out of scope. The audit is itself a model reading your files, so review its suggestions like any other output. Not checked: an OpenCode equivalent.
Write the file yourself first and read what /init produces critically. A generated file can contain wrong guesses about your project.

Write a short instructions file (about ten lines) for one of your real projects: how to run its tests, where data lives, and one thing the agent should leave alone.
