title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
Prerequisites: The Context Window. Objective: use six terms precisely (token, context window, session context, memory, session usage, context poisoning), and say what to do when a wrong claim has got into a session or into memory. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): research/failure-modes.md sources on 2026-11-16 (Claude Code memory, sessions, costs, commands and best-practices docs). Claude Code specific unless stated. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
People say “it remembers”, “the session got long” and “I hit my usage” as if these were one thing. They are different things, with different places they live and different ways to reset them. Think of a lab glossary: one term, one meaning.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
The glossary
Token. A chunk of text the model reads (a word piece, a character or a byte). Context limits and usage are counted in tokens. Details are in Tokens, Not Letters.
Context window. Everything the model can see when it writes its next output. It has a size limit, measured in tokens. See The Context Window.
Session and session context. A session is a saved conversation tied to a project directory (stored locally as a transcript file). Its session context is what is in the window right now. The docs say each session begins with a fresh context window and that sessions are independent: a new session has no history from earlier ones.
Memory. Text on disk that is read into a new window at the start of every session. In Claude Code there are two kinds, both loaded at session start:

CLAUDE.md: instructions you write (scope = who or where a setting applies: project, user or organisation).
Auto memory: notes the harness writes itself from your corrections and preferences. It is per git repository and machine-local, kept in ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/ as plain markdown with a MEMORY.md index. Only the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md load at start; topic files are read on demand.

Memory is advisory context, and it takes room in the window every session. Run /clear and the conversation goes while memory stays. Compaction shrinks a session and leaves memory as it was.
Session usage. How much of your allowance a session consumes. In Claude Code, /usage shows an estimated session cost (worked out locally from token counts at list price, the published per-token price), plan usage limits and activity stats. /cost and /stats are aliases. The displayed session total resets on /clear; whether allowance already spent on a plan comes back is not documented (our inference: it does not). Two billing worlds exist: with a subscription, the plan bars are what matter and the dollar figure is an estimate (plans have rolling and weekly limit windows; see your plan docs, as the docs we read confirm the exact windows only for Teams and Enterprise per-seat allowances); with the API, usage is billed per token, and thinking tokens (the tokens the model spends reasoning before it answers) count as output tokens. The docs do not state allowance sizes for the individual plans, so see the vendor’s pricing page.
Context poisoning. A wrong or injected statement enters the context and later answers build on it. This is a community term from outside vendor documentation. It was coined in the post “How Long Contexts Fail” (2025-06-22) credited to Drew Breunig (the byline comes from a reprint listing; the page text we read did not name him). His example is a game-playing agent whose recorded goals became corrupted with false state. We found no use of this term in Anthropic’s docs; they do describe the same trap in plain words, below.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
Side by side









Term
Lives where
Survives /clear?
You control it by




Session context
The window, this session only
No
/clear, /compact, what you let in


CLAUDE.md
A file you write
Yes
Editing the file


Auto memory
Markdown files the tool writes
Yes
/memory (read, edit, delete, toggle)


Session cost display
Counted locally from tokens sent
Displayed total resets; plan limit use already spent does not come back (our inference)
Smaller outputs, fewer subagents (helper agents with their own context window), /clear between tasks


Poisoned claim
In the context, or in memory
Gone from the context, stays in memory
Fresh session; delete the memory line

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
Why usage climbs
The docs give these reasons. Claude Code sends the whole conversation on every request, and each tool-using step is another request. Caching (a short-term store so repeated text is cheaper to re-read) makes re-reading cheaper but a short question late in a long session still draws on all of it. Large tool outputs (the docs’ example is reading a 10,000-line log) stay in the conversation. Subagents each have their own context, and their requests still count. /compact itself reads the whole conversation. Remedies from the docs: /clear between unrelated tasks, /compact with a focus note, /context to see what fills the window, and keeping CLAUDE.md under 200 lines.
Seeing “rate limited until …” in /usage means the tool could not fetch plan limits, and says nothing about your work being limited.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
section: When a wrong claim gets in
text:
When a wrong claim gets in
Anthropic’s best-practices guidance is plain: if you have corrected the same thing twice and it is still wrong, /clear plus one new prompt that folds in what you learned works well, since a third correction mostly adds to a conversation that already holds two failed attempts for the model to re-read. /rewind can roll back to before the bad turn.
Memory persists, so a wrong line costs the most there. General practice (our inference, from no official instruction): do not let a claim into CLAUDE.md or auto memory until you have checked it against the source, such as the data, the tool’s --help or the paper. If a bad line is already there, open /memory, read what has been written about your project, and delete it.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands the docs confirm: /memory (lists memory files, toggles auto memory, opens the folder), /clear (new empty conversation; the old one stays resumable), /compact, /resume and claude --resume (pick an earlier session), claude --continue (most recent in this directory), /usage, /context. Resume restores messages, model and permission mode (what the agent may do without asking), and leaves startup flags such as --mcp-config for you to pass again. Transcripts are deleted after 30 days by default.


Not checked: OpenCode’s memory files, session commands and usage reporting. The research for this page covers Claude Code only. General practice: with a local Ollama model the window is still finite, so the ideas about session context and poisoned claims carry over; find your tool’s own commands in its documentation. Not checked: whether anything is billed per token by a vendor.




If you use a tool with memory, open it (in Claude Code, /memory) and read what it has recorded about a project. Is every line something you could source?


In a session you already have, run /usage and note what dominates: long conversation, big outputs or subagents. If it is not available to you, skip this.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
Prerequisites: When to Start Fresh. Objective: triage each new thought during a task into the right place (do now, park, quick question, helper, branch, or later session), and know what undo can and cannot restore. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): research/session-management.md sources on 2026-11-16 (Claude Code commands, sessions, worktrees, checkpointing and best-practices docs). Claude Code specific unless stated. Parking-lot files are general practice. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
Real work does not arrive in a straight line. You start fixing a samplesheet parser and think: “should I switch the aligner? What if I tried a stricter QC threshold? I also want to explore that other idea.” If you type every one of those into the same conversation, the context (everything the model can see when it writes its next reply, see The Context Window) fills with side tracks. Anthropic’s writing on context says accuracy and recall degrade as context grows, and the docs say the whole conversation is re-sent on every request, so a cluttered session tends to cost more per step (not checked: how much usage each route below saves; the research documents the mechanisms but gives no numbers). This is how a session ends up with three unrelated tasks that it “re-reads on every turn of the fourth”, in the docs’ words. A turn is one prompt from you plus the model’s reply.
Ideas are welcome. The fix is to triage each one.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
Terms used here

Session: one saved conversation with the tool, tied to a project folder.
Subagent: a helper the main agent starts. It works in its own separate, clean context (it knows what you tell it) and sends back a summary, so its reading stays out of your conversation.
Conversation branch (/branch, which is separate from a git branch): a copy of the conversation from this point, so you can try something in the copy while the original stays as it was. /fork is a different command: it copies the conversation into a separate background session.
Git worktree: a second checkout of the same repository in another folder, so two sessions can edit files without overwriting each other.
Checkpoint: a snapshot Claude Code takes at each prompt you send, so you can roll back with /rewind.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
The triage
For each new thought, ask in this order. The key question is step 2: do you want the answer or the work during this session? If not, park it. If you do, steps 3 to 6 are the ways to get it.

Does it block the current task? Do it now, in this session.
Do you not want the answer or the work this session? Park it: write one line in a file and carry on (general practice, see below). Parked ideas leave through the “later session” exit: once the current task is done, pick from the file.
You want it now: is it a quick question you do not need on record? Use /btw <question>. It sees the conversation so far, has no tool access (it cannot read files, run commands or look at --help) and adds nothing to the history. So it suits questions about this conversation. An answer about a tool’s flags or defaults comes from the model’s memory: verify it against --help or the docs.
You want it now: is it exploration where you only need a summary? Ask for a subagent (it starts with its own clean context; the built-in Explore helper is a fast read-only searcher), or use /subtask <task>, which starts a background helper that inherits the whole conversation and returns its result here.
You want it now: is it a competing approach you want to try for real? Use /branch [name] to copy the conversation (the original stays reachable via /resume), or start a second session in its own worktree with claude --worktree <name>.
You want it now: is it a different task entirely? Finish the current one, commit your work, then /clear or start a new named session (claude -n <name>, or /rename <name> inside one).









New thought
Where it goes
Why




“The parser crashes on this sample ID” (it is the task)
Do now
It blocks you


“Maybe a stricter QC threshold would help”
Parking-lot line
You do not want the answer this session; no cost to the context


“Which sample did we exclude earlier?”
/btw
One answer from the conversation; no tools; stays out of the history


“Where is the aligner configured across the repo?”
Explore subagent or /subtask
Heavy reading stays out of your main context; you get a summary


“Try the other aligner and compare”
/branch or claude --worktree <name>
A real attempt that can fail without spoiling the main path


“Redo the plots for the other project” (you want to start it now)
Commit, then /clear or a new named session
Different task, different files, different context

title: The Stream of Ideas
section: What is and is not shared
text:
What is and is not shared
A worktree session isolates file edits only. Per the docs, claude --worktree <name> creates .claude/worktrees/<name>/ on a branch called worktree-<name>. Worktrees share the repository’s .git, and auto memory is per repository, so all worktrees share it. A fresh checkout does not contain gitignored files such as .env unless you list them in .worktreeinclude, and large data folders need worktree.symlinkDirectories or a setup step. Plan for that before you start a pipeline test in one.
/branch copies the conversation. Any background helpers still running keep reporting into the branch.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
Checkpoints and /rewind
Every prompt you send is a checkpoint. /rewind (aliases /checkpoint, /undo; or press Esc twice on an empty prompt) lets you restore code and conversation, only the conversation, or only the code. The limits matter to bioinformatics: files changed only through Bash (the shell command tool) are not tracked, subagent edits are mostly not restored, and edits outside the session are not tracked. The docs say checkpoints are “not a replacement for version control”. A sed -i or a script that rewrites a results table is a Bash change (our inference from the limits), so exploring is safe only after you have committed.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
A parking-lot file
General practice (our inference, not a documented feature): no official page describes a parking-lot file. Keep it outside what the agent reads every session; the research cautions that a file imported into your instructions costs context each time. Keep it in the repository if the team should see it, in a gitignored file if it is personal, or use an issue tracker for anything that outlives the week.
# IDEAS.md  (one line each: date | idea | why it matters | revisit when)
2026-11-16 | Add a --dry-run flag to the parser | Check a samplesheet without writing output | after parser fix is merged
2026-11-16 | Stricter QC threshold (Q30 not Q20) | Fewer false variants in low-depth samples | when the test cohort is ready
2026-11-16 | Per-sample coverage plot | Spot dropouts faster | before the next batch

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
Worked example
You are fixing a samplesheet parser that rejects sample IDs containing a dot.

“Does the pipeline require the dot at all?” That blocks the fix: do it now.
“Would a stricter QC threshold help?” You do not want the answer today: park it as a line in IDEAS.md.
“Which sample did we exclude earlier?” A quick question about this conversation: /btw. (Had it been “what does --min-qual default to?”, /btw could only guess from memory, so you would check --help instead.)
“Where else do we split sample IDs on dots?” Wide reading, only the list matters: Explore subagent.
“Let’s try the other aligner and compare.” A real experiment you want now: commit the fix, then /branch or a worktree session.
“I should also tidy the figures for the other project.” A different task you will start once the parser is done: later session: commit, /clear, or claude -n figures.

The main session ended with the parser fixed and a short, readable history.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands the docs confirm: /btw, /subtask, /branch, /fork, /rewind, /clear, /rename, /resume, claude -n <name>, claude --worktree <name> (or -w). Plan mode (/plan, or Shift+Tab until the bar shows it) makes Claude read and propose without editing until you approve. General practice (our inference): it suits a side idea you only want to think through.


Not checked: OpenCode’s side-question, branch and worktree features; the research could not find its share and fork pages. Documented on its terminal page: /new (alias /clear) for a fresh session, /sessions to return to one, /compact, and /undo and /redo (these need a git repository). General practice: a parking-lot file and a commit before exploring work in any tool, local models included.




Start a parking-lot file (or open an issue list) for your current project and add the three ideas on your mind, one line each with a reason and a trigger to revisit.


Look back at your last long session. Pick one side thought you followed and say where the triage would have sent it.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
text:
Prerequisites: Who Said What. This is an optional side quest; Plug In a Server (advised) puts it to use. Objective: explain why a large toolset costs context and accuracy, and choose between a single call, a fixed workflow, an agent, and a plain script. Time: about 20 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude API tool-search docs, Claude Code MCP docs and Anthropic’s “Building effective agents” article on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/fundamentals.md). The figures quoted are Anthropic’s own claims and were not measured here. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
Every tool you give an agent has a definition: a name and a description of how to use it. The model needs those definitions in its window to choose a tool. That is the cost this quest is about, followed by the related question of whether you need an agent at all.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
text:
Tools cost context
Anthropic’s tool-search docs say loading every tool definition up front causes context bloat. As an example they give a typical five-server setup that can use about 55 thousand tokens in definitions before any work starts. They also say Claude’s ability to pick the right tool degrades once you exceed 30 to 50 available tools. These are Anthropic’s statements on a docs page, with no method given, so read them as a rough guide to the shape of the problem; no thresholds were measured.
The same docs describe tool search: keep most definitions out of the window and load a few on demand. They say it typically cuts that overhead by over 85 percent, and they advise it from about 10 tools upward, or when definitions are large. Below that, plain tool calling is better.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Per the docs, MCP tool search is on by default: tool names and server instructions load at session start, and a full definition loads when needed (deferred). So extra MCP servers have a small effect on the window. It can be turned off with ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false, and on some older models it falls back to loading everything. Skills work the same way in spirit: descriptions load at start. /context shows what takes space. Whether the 30 to 50 tool accuracy claim still applies behind deferral is not stated in the docs we read.


Not checked: whether OpenCode defers tool definitions. Assume tool definitions cost context until you know otherwise, and keep the set small, especially on a local model with a small window (general practice).



The habit that follows (general practice, inferred from the above): few, clearly named tools, and remove the servers you do not use.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
section: Single call, workflow, agent, or script
text:
Single call, workflow, agent, or script
Anthropic’s article “Building effective agents” separates two things. A workflow orchestrates models and tools through paths fixed in code. An agent is a system where the model directs its own process and tool use. The article’s advice is to start with the simplest solution that works, and it says that building no agentic system (one where the model picks its own steps and tools) at all may be the right choice. For many uses, one well-prepared call is usually enough. It adds that agents trade speed and cost for performance, and that autonomy brings compounding errors, so test with limits: a stopping condition such as a maximum number of steps.
Our reading of that, as general practice:

A plain script when the rule is known. Counting reads, converting a format, running fastqc then trim then align in a fixed order. A Nextflow pipeline is already a workflow.
A single call when you paste the input and want a text answer, such as explaining an error.
An agent when the next step depends on what it finds, such as debugging a failing run or exploring an unfamiliar repository. Even then, give it a way to check its own work and a limit.

Using none of these is also a fine decision.

List the MCP servers and tools in your setup. For each, say when you last used it. Remove or disable one you do not need.


Take one task you gave an agent that had a known rule. Write down the script that would do it without a model.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
Prerequisites: Tokens, Not Letters. Objective: sort jobs into “ask the model” and “run a script”, and name the other ways a model fails with one mitigation each. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): the sources listed in research/failure-modes.md (sections 6 and 7) on 2026-11-16. Verified: ran echo banana | grep -o n | wc -l and grep -c '>' on a three-record mock file. Items marked “general practice” or “Not checked:” are not from a source. Topics in this zone were inspired by Matt Pocock’s course LLM Fundamentals (aihero.dev/llm-fundamentals). The explanations here are our own.
A language model is good at some jobs and bad at others. The skill is knowing which is which before you trust the output. Using a model is always your choice. This quest shows where the risk sits if you do.

title: Where Machines Fail
section: Good jobs: the result is checkable
text:
Good jobs: the result is checkable
Models are generally useful where you can read the result, or run it, and judge it yourself (our inference from the research notes):

summarising text
drafting prose, such as a README or a methods first draft
explaining code or an error message
converting formats, for example a samplesheet CSV to JSON (a structured text format)
first drafts of code that you will then test

Caveat for summaries. A summary can leave things out or bend them. A peer-reviewed study of the older, pre-chat generation of summarisation models (Maynez et al., ACL 2020) found substantial unfaithful content in every system tested. That evidence is dated; the direction still applies. We found no published faithfulness rate for current Claude on scientific papers. So spot-check against the source: numbers, gene and sample names, direction of effect, negations. Omissions are harder to see, so skim the abstract and limitations yourself. Asking the model to quote the supporting lines first also helps; the Anthropic docs recommend quote-first extraction.

title: Where Machines Fail
section: Bad job: exact counting and arithmetic
text:
Bad job: exact counting and arithmetic
Ask a model: “How many n are in banana?” The right answer is 2 (b-a-n-a-n-a). A model can get this wrong, and can be wrong while sounding sure (see the overconfidence row below). A leading explanation is the one from the last quest: it reads tokens, which are chunks of letters (see Tokens, Not Letters). The state of the science is mixed. Some papers propose tokenisation as the cause (arXiv 2505.14172, arXiv 2410.19730), and another study (CharBench, arXiv 2508.02591) finds it only weakly related to correctness, with word length and the true count mattering more. The cause is debated. The fix works whichever cause is right.
The fix is to run a script. Verified: ran this on macOS:
echo banana | grep -o n | wc -l
It printed 2 (the macOS wc pads with spaces; the number is 2). One preprint (arXiv 2410.14166, by Xu and Ma; its full text, not its abstract) reports that coding models asked to write Python for such counting tasks do them perfectly, while the same models fail when answering open-endedly. General practice: so for exact counts, have the model write the script and read the script and its output. Treat a count it states from “doing the sum in its head” as a guess to check.
The bioinformatics versions of the same trap:







You want
Give it to




Number of sequences in a FASTA
grep -c '>' file.fa (Verified: ran on a three-record mock file, printed 3), or seqkit stats


GC content, read length statistics
a script, run by the agent, with the code visible


A p-value or any test statistic
a stats library in a script you can read and re-run


Sum or mean of a column
awk, or a script that prints the number; a number stated in prose is a guess



Rule of thumb: ask for the command and its output, and treat a count stated in prose as a guess to check.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


It can run Bash (the shell command tool) and write scripts, so ask: “write and run a command for this, and show me both the command and its output.”


Same rule. Not checked: how reliable small local models are at this. General practice: assume they count about as poorly, and ask for a script.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
Other ways it fails









Failure mode
What it looks like
What to do
Quest




Hallucination
A confident statement that is false. For example a plausible DOI, gene ID or tool flag that does not exist
Allow “I don’t know”; ask for word-for-word quotes first; restrict to supplied documents; look up every ID in PubMed or Ensembl, or run the tool’s --help
Spot the Mirage


Sycophancy
Telling you what you want to hear. It agrees with your wrong hypothesis, or softens a correct criticism when you push back (Sharma et al., arXiv 2310.13548)
General practice: ask for the strongest case against your idea, and hold back your preferred answer
none yet


Long-context degradation
Accuracy and recall drop as input grows (“context rot”, per Anthropic’s docs: the longer the input, the worse the recall); relevant text in the middle is used less (arXiv 2307.03172)
Curate input: head, counts, filtered tables; start fresh for a new task
The Context Window


Instruction drift
An early instruction is forgotten, for example after compaction (the harness replacing old conversation with a summary to free room)
Short instructions file (CLAUDE.md or similar, loaded at session start); a hook for must-never rules (Claude Code)
The Context Window


Non-determinism
The same prompt can give different answers
Not checked in the official docs. General practice: run twice and compare; record command, model and version; treat the script it wrote as the reproducible part
Same Every Time


Overconfidence
Reports a task as done while it is unfinished, often because it had no way to check
Give it a check to run (tests, row counts, md5) and read the output
none yet


Prompt injection
Text from fetched content that the model treats as an instruction. For example a README, PDF or FASTA header contains instructions the agent follows
Treat fetched content as data; review commands before approving; no system is fully immune
Plug In a Server


Stale knowledge
Newer tool versions or database releases postdate its training
Check --version and the current docs. Current Claude models list a June 2026 cutoff
none yet

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
The decision rule
Can I check the result cheaply and independently? If yes, ask the model: a bad answer is likely to show (omissions may not, so check those deliberately). If the answer must be exactly right and cannot be checked, use a script.

Ask a model to count one letter in a long word (or a mock 40-letter DNA string), then check it with grep -o and wc -l. Note whether it was right, and how sure it sounded. One try is a demonstration and falls short of proof.


Have a model summarise a methods paragraph you wrote. Check every number, name and negation against your original, and note anything omitted.

title: Grow the Carapace
text:
Prerequisites: Recruit the Beast, or Adopt the Pet if you only run a local model. Objective: write permission rules that hold, and know where they stop holding. Time: about 20 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code v2.1.323 and OpenCode v2.3.0 on 2026-11-13 (sources in research/kennel-and-crypt.md).
The harness (the program around the model) enforces rules. A line in your instructions file (such as CLAUDE.md) asking the agent to avoid something is guidance, and it does not change what is allowed.
Sort every action into three bins: allow (safe and routine), ask (you want to decide each time), deny (never).

title: Grow the Carapace
text:
Where the carapace has gaps

Rules that match command arguments are fragile: Bash(rm *) does not match /bin/rm or bash -c 'rm ...'.
Claude Code’s sandbox is off by default. When on, it limits shell commands only; file tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside it, and by default it can still read ~/.ssh.
Your secrets in environment variables are inherited by the commands it runs.

Treat rules as one layer. Git (your save point) and a throwaway folder are the others.

title: Bundle a Plugin
text:
Prerequisites: Test the Skill. This is an optional side quest. Objective: package Skills (and their evals) as a plugin, validate it, and know why installing one is a trust decision. Time: about 20 minutes. Verified: ran claude plugin validate . and --strict on exercises/forge/fasta-tools (Claude Code 2.1.325). Other claims: last verified (docs, not run) on 2026-11-13, sources in research/forge.md.
A single Skill in your folder helps you. A plugin is a folder that bundles Skills, and optionally agents, hooks and MCP servers (add-on connections that give the agent extra tools), so a whole group can install the same set and get updates.

title: Bundle a Plugin
section: Installing one is a trust decision
text:
Installing one is a trust decision






Warning



Per the Claude Code docs, a plugin you install can run arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges. Hooks, monitors, local MCP and language servers, and anything in bin/ run outside the sandbox and the permission rules. Skills and agents enter the context as instructions, and instructions can steer the agent too.


Before installing or updating a plugin:

Check where it comes from. A marketplace name says who publishes it. Reading the plugin shows what it does.
Read hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json, and anything in bin/. These are where code lives.
In a session, /plugin shows what will be installed. claude --plugin-dir <dir> plugin details <name> lists a component inventory without a session.
Remember that auto-update can change files you reviewed. Pin a version for plugins you publish.

title: Bundle a Plugin
text:
When a team shares Skills
Idea from the GitHub Blog article “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” by Andrea Griffiths (GitHub Blog), in our own words. It is advice for teams and sits outside the plugin format.

Keep project names and conventions in one file. The reference genome build, the sample-ID pattern and the results folder names belong in a single project-facts file (a plain file that lists them, separate from the plugin’s plugin.json) which every Skill reads, so no SKILL.md repeats them. Then another lab can reuse your Skills with its own file and no rewriting, and a rename touches one place.
Keep discovered details apart from team standards. A pattern the agent finds in your code is an observation. Store it separately, and have a person confirm it before it becomes a standard.
If you generate copies, check for drift. Say you keep one source SKILL.md and generate copies for other tools. Run a check in CI (automated checks that run on every change) that fails when a copy no longer matches its source.
Blocking a merge depends on repository rules and required checks. Whether a bad change is stopped depends on those rules. A review step written in a Skill is advice unless a required check backs it.


Turn the Skill you wrote into a plugin folder with a plugin.json, then run claude plugin validate on it and read the output.

title: Forge a Skill
text:
Prerequisites: The Project Charter. Plan Before You Edit is advised. Objective: package a repeatable procedure as a Skill, and know what a Skill covers and where its limits lie. Time: about 20 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code v2.1.323 and OpenCode docs (they describe V2; installed version not checked) on 2026-11-13 (sources in research/forest-and-reef.md and research/doctor.md).
An instructions file is read every session. A Skill is a procedure loaded only when it is relevant, so it can be long without crowding the context.

title: Forge a Skill
text:
What a Skill is
A Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file. Only each Skill’s short description is preloaded. The body is read when the Skill is used. A Skill can also bundle scripts and other files. In Claude Code, both you (by name, such as /check-fasta) and the agent (by matching the description) can start one.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Place it at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (project) or ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (all projects). All frontmatter fields (frontmatter: the settings block between the two --- lines at the top of the file) are optional, but write a clear description so it triggers at the right time. Keep the body under about 500 lines. The older .claude/commands/ format still works but is merged into Skills.


OpenCode reads skills from .opencode/skills, .claude/skills and .agents/skills, so the same SKILL.md can serve both tools. Custom agents live in .opencode/agents/*.md.



An example you can write by hand in a scratch folder:
---
name: check-fasta
description: Count the records in a FASTA file and find duplicate IDs. Use before running any analysis on a new FASTA.
---

1. Run `grep -c '>' FILE` to count records.
2. Run `grep '>' FILE | sort | uniq -d` to find duplicate IDs.
3. Report what you ran and its output. Leave FILE unchanged.

title: Forge a Skill
section: Do it: install it, then confirm it loaded
text:
Do it: install it, then confirm it loaded
Writing the file is half the job. A Skill with a typo in its frontmatter loads silently with no fields set, so always check.

In a scratch folder (never a real project), save the example above as .claude/skills/check-fasta/SKILL.md. The --- must be the very first line of the file.
Make a tiny test file: printf '>a\nACGT\n>a\nGGCC\n' > reads.fa (two records, one duplicated ID).
Confirm the tool can see it:


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Start claude in the scratch folder. Type / and look for check-fasta in the menu, or run /skills. If you created a top-level skills folder after the session started, run /reload-skills. Then ask in plain words, leaving the Skill unnamed: “I just got reads.fa from a collaborator. Is it OK to analyse?” The agent should load the Skill and report the commands it ran.


Start opencode in the scratch folder. OpenCode finds .claude/skills too. The model loads a Skill through its skill tool, and you can load one yourself by writing @check-fasta in a prompt. Then ask the same question and check whether the Skill was used.




If it did not trigger, check in this order: the file starts with --- on line 1; the YAML (the key: value text format used in that block) parses; field names are spelled right; the description says when to use it, with the key use case first (long descriptions are cut off in the listing).

A Skill that is listed but never picked up is a finding about the description or the prompt. Next you will learn to measure that.
If a Skill never fires, two slash commands (a /command typed inside the running tool) help you look. /skills lists the skills the tool can see, and t sorts them by token count (how many tokens, the chunks of text a model reads, each one takes). /skill-doctor (v2.1.252 or later) shows each skill’s context cost (how much of the model’s limited reading space its text takes up) and how often it is used, and flags skills that sit in the listing but are never invoked. It excludes bundled and enterprise skills.






Warning



In Claude Code, allowed-tools in a Skill pre-approves tools for that turn (one prompt and its reply). Other tools stay available to the agent. A Skill offers no sandbox, and a Skill you download is code you choose to trust. Read it before installing it, as you would read a script.

title: Forge a Skill
section: Design the Skill like a small job
text:
Design the Skill like a small job
Idea from the GitHub Blog article “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” by Andrea Griffiths (GitHub Blog). The points below are our own wording of its advice, and the Agent Skills standard itself is outside the article’s scope.

One Skill, one job. Give it a defined input (what it is handed, such as a FASTA path) and a defined output (what it must return, such as a count and a list of duplicate IDs). If you need “and also” in the description, you probably have two Skills.
Say what it does and when to use it. The name and description should state the task and its purpose. In the body, add a short When to use part, and a What evidence to report part (the commands run and their output), so a reviewer can see what happened.
Start from a task you keep explaining. If you re-explain the same check each session, such as how to confirm a FASTQ file has no truncated records, that check is your first Skill. Write down its inputs, its limits and what a reviewer needs to see.
A Skill describes the method. The tool that runs it still supplies the tools, credentials and permissions. A Skill that says “submit this to the cluster” brings no cluster account or allocation with it.
Know when a Skill is the wrong fit. Skills suit bounded, repeatable work such as a pre-submission checklist for a samplesheet. Work that needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail or permissions enforced from outside, such as a lab’s shared sample-tracking service, suits an application (a separate program with its own tests and access rules) better than instructions.

Portability. The Claude Code and OpenCode docs listed in Lore below say both read .claude/skills, so one SKILL.md can serve both. The article’s advice, which is a sensible habit, is to verify in each client (the tool that runs the agent, such as Claude Code or OpenCode) you use after installing: does it trigger on the right request, load the files the Skill refers to, use the tools it needs, and return the evidence you asked for? Clients differ in models, tools and permissions, so a Skill that works in one can fail in another.

Write a SKILL.md for one chore you repeat (checking an input, summarising a log). Make the description say when to use it.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Prerequisites: Close the Loop. Objective: read and write a small Claude Code eval case that checks a Skill is triggered, and know what running it costs. Time: about 20 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code v2.1.325 plugin-evals docs on 2026-11-13 (sources in research/forge.md). claude plugin eval was not run for this page.
Words used below. Grader: a check that marks a run pass or fail. Arm: one condition of the comparison (with the plugin, or without). Ablation: removing the thing to see what changes. Judge model: a second model that marks the answer. Baseline: the run without the change.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Where this works
claude plugin eval needs Claude Code v2.1.269 or later. It evaluates a plugin directory (a folder with .claude-plugin/plugin.json), so first turn your Skill into a small plugin; the next quest covers bundling in more detail. The example exercises/forge/fasta-tools in this repository already has the shape:
fasta-tools/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json
├── skills/check-fasta/SKILL.md
└── evals/skill-triggers/
    ├── prompt.md
    └── graders/skill-fired.md

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


The case is a prompt plus one or more graders. The prompt is written the way a user would ask, and leaves the Skill unnamed:
---
runs: 1
---
I just got a new FASTA file called reads.fa from a collaborator. Can you check it is OK before I start the analysis?
The grader is a free check on the transcript, with no model call. It passes if the Skill tool was invoked for check-fasta:
---
type: tool_used
tool: Skill
input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?check-fasta"'
---
The check-fasta skill should be used when the user asks to check a new FASTA file, without naming the skill.
Run it cheaply while you iterate, one case, one run, no baseline arm:
claude plugin eval . --case skill-triggers --runs 1 --ablation none
The full comparison runs each case three times by default, with the plugin (WITH) and without it (W/OUT), and reports the difference (Δ):
claude plugin eval . --max-cost-usd 2
--max-cost-usd stops the run at a ceiling. Results land in evals/results/<timestamp>/ with a report.html.


Last verified (docs): the pages read describe OpenCode skills and plugins but no equivalent of claude plugin eval. Treat that as unconfirmed. You can still do the same comparison by hand: run one prompt several times with the Skill folder present, several times with it moved away, and compare using a script that checks the output. A small local model is cheap to run this way, but it follows Skills less reliably, so expect noisier results.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Reading the result

Six grader types exist. Four are free and computed from the transcript or files (regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists). Two use a judge model and cost tokens (llm, baseline; the baseline grader type is a different thing from the baseline run). Graders come from these six types only.
In a two-arm run, tool_used: Skill is shown as an indicator and counts towards the score only when you set arm: both.
Δ near zero with the Skill not firing is usually a real finding: the description does not trigger on that phrasing. Change the description, not the grader.
Pair one result grader with one process grader. Use llm graders only for short output, with a concrete PASS/FAIL rubric.
Each run happens in an isolated child session (a separate session started just for that run) with only the plugin loaded, so personal settings, the instructions file and other plugins are absent. Behaviour in your own setup may differ from a pass there.
claude plugin validate checks that the files are well formed. Behaviour needs an eval.







Note



Running an eval is the same trust decision as loading the plugin with --plugin-dir. Hooks you did not write still run code. Safety needs a review of its own, which a passing eval does not replace.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Who checks the work
Idea from the GitHub Blog article “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” by Andrea Griffiths (GitHub Blog), in our own words. The grader and baseline method above comes from the Claude Code docs.

Use a separate verifier, a check done by something other than the agent that did the work. An agent that marks its own work gives a self-check. For a QC skill that edits a samplesheet, have a script or a person diff the changed file against the original, and make the verifier cite the lines it relied on.
Check the Skill in each client you use (the tool that runs the agent, such as Claude Code or OpenCode). Passing in one tool says little about another. After installing, confirm that the client triggers the Skill for the right task, loads its files, uses the tools it needs and returns the evidence you expect.
Instructions guide; tests and people verify. A line in a Skill saying “check your work” steers the agent. Tests, CI checks (continuous integration: automatic checks that run when code is pushed) and human review verify.


Run the cheap one-case command above on exercises/forge/fasta-tools with a cost ceiling, and open the report.html. Note whether the Skill fired.


Write an eval case for your own Skill from the previous quest: a prompt that leaves it unnamed, and one grader.

title: Write the Brief
text:
Prerequisites: Recruit the Beast. The Context Window is advised. Objective: write prompts that make output checkable, and manage the context window so the agent stays on task. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code v2.1.323 and OpenCode docs (they describe V2; installed version not checked) on 2026-11-13 (sources in research/forest-and-reef.md).
The first branch of the skill tree is the brief: what you tell the agent. A vague brief invites a plausible guess. A good brief names the file and the symptom, says what “done” looks like, and gives the agent a check it can run.
Two habits make the rest of this safer:

title: Write the Brief
text:
Context is a budget
Everything in the conversation takes up room in the context window. The Claude Code docs note that old conversation can crowd out the files you need next.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


/context shows what is filling the window. /compact summarises the conversation (you can say what to keep). /clear starts fresh, which is right when you switch to an unrelated task. Claude Code also compacts automatically near the limit.


/compact (alias /summarize, meaning another name for the same command) summarises the session and /new (alias /clear) starts a new one. The docs show no /context equivalent in the TUI (the text user interface, OpenCode’s terminal screen).

title: Guard the Door
text:
Prerequisites: Plug In a Server. Objective: write a hook that refuses a command, and know where a hook’s coverage ends. Time: about 15 minutes. Last verified (docs, not run): Claude Code docs and OpenCode V2 docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in research/tools-and-guards.md)
A hook is a user-defined handler that runs automatically at a set point in the harness’s lifecycle. In Claude Code it can be a shell command, an HTTP endpoint and other kinds, and it receives JSON (a structured text format) about the event. An instructions file asks the model to behave. A command hook is ordinary code that the harness runs, so what it decides does not depend on what the model wants. That contrast is our inference from how exit code 2 works (a nonzero exit code is how a script signals failure; a hook uses 2 to mean block), not a phrase from the docs.

title: Guard the Door
text:
A hook that refuses

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Hooks go in a hooks block in a settings file. .claude/settings.json is committable and shared, .claude/settings.local.json is yours alone, and ~/.claude/settings.json covers all projects. A PreToolUse hook fires before a tool runs, and the matcher (the pattern that selects which tool the hook fires for) Bash selects the shell tool:
{ "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash",
  "hooks": [ { "type": "command",
    "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/block-drop-table.sh" } ] } ] } }
The script, as in the Claude Code hooks guide (short third-party text, quoted with attribution). It needs jq installed to read the JSON, and it must be executable (check the guide for the exact step; chmod +x is the usual way):
#!/bin/bash
INPUT=$(cat)
COMMAND=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command')
if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q "drop table"; then
  echo "Blocked: dropping tables is not allowed" >&2  # stderr becomes Claude's feedback
  exit 2                                               # exit 2 = block the action
fi
exit 0  # exit 0 = no decision; the normal permission flow applies
The hook gets the event as JSON on stdin (its standard input), including tool_name and, for Bash, tool_input.command. Exit code 2 on PreToolUse blocks the call, and Claude sees the stderr text (the program’s error output) as the reason. Exit 0 expresses no decision: the call goes through the normal permission flow.
Two behaviours matter for trust. First, if the script crashes or exits with some other code and prints no valid JSON, the action proceeds on most events. A broken guard fails open (it lets the action through when it breaks), unless the hook is configured to block on failure (the guide names onFailure: "block"; check the current docs for where it goes). Second, exit 2 blocks on some events only: on PostToolUse the tool already ran and exit 2 shows stderr to Claude, and on Notification the exit code is ignored.


The V2 docs describe plugins (files under .opencode/plugins/ or ~/.config/opencode/plugins/) that can register hooks. For refusing an action, the documented route is the permission hook, ctx.permission.hook("evaluate", ...): it runs for allow and ask decisions, may change the effect to allow, ask or deny, and event.message is the denial reason. An explicit configured deny is final and never invokes the hook.
Not checked: an exit-code-2 equivalent or shell-hook configuration (neither appears in the pages read), and whether throwing from a tool hook blocks a call (the docs leave it undescribed, so do not rely on it until you have verified it). Not checked: a trust statement for plugins; treat them as code running with your privileges, which is an inference. Not checked: how any of this behaves with a local Ollama model. Check your installed version’s docs.

title: Guard the Door
text:
What a hook covers

Not a sandbox. The example matches the literal string “drop table” in one command. A matcher selects by tool name, not by content. If the model runs a script that contains the dangerous command, or spells it differently, a grep on the command text never sees it (our inference; the docs do not discuss evasion).
Fires only on tool calls. PreToolUse fires when Claude calls a tool. A file added with an @ reference in your prompt is read without a tool call, so no hook fires.
Cannot override your deny and ask rules. A hook returning allow skips the prompt, and deny and ask rules are still evaluated.
Runs with your full permissions. The docs say command hooks “execute shell commands with your full user permissions”, so review and test them before adding them.

title: Guard the Door
section: A hook in a repository is code you did not write
text:
A hook in a repository is code you did not write
If a repository commits hooks in .claude/settings.json, they are code from its authors, running as you. Interactive Claude Code holds hooks back until you accept the workspace trust dialog. In -p and SDK runs (headless: non-interactive, no one to answer a dialog) there is no dialog, and the docs say hooks committed in a repository’s .claude/settings.json run in a folder you have never trusted. Read .claude/ before running headless in a clone, and the docs name --bare and disableAllHooks as ways to switch them off.

In a throwaway folder with mock files, add the Bash-blocking hook above and ask for a harmless command that contains “drop table” in an echo. Note the stderr message the agent reports. Then change the script to exit 1 and see what happens.

title: Adopt the Pet
text:
Prerequisites: Save Point, a laptop with about 16 GB of memory, a terminal, and roughly 5 GB of free disk. This is an optional side quest. WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) users: see the unconfirmed list at the end. Objective: run a small local model with Ollama, give it enough context, and point OpenCode at it. Time: about 20 minutes. Everything stays on your machine.
Last verified (docs, not run): Ollama v0.40.16 and OpenCode v2.3.0 on 2026-11-13. Sources: research/kennel-and-crypt.md






Warning



Some details on this page are unconfirmed. They are listed at the end under “Unconfirmed”.

title: Adopt the Pet
text:
The Pet
A small local model is gentle, free, and private. It also forgets things quickly and gets things wrong more often than a large hosted model. That is fine if you know it.

title: Adopt the Pet
section: 1. Install Ollama and fetch a model
text:
1. Install Ollama and fetch a model
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh     # macOS and Linux
ollama pull qwen3:4b                              # about 2.5 GB
ollama run qwen3:4b "Say hello in one sentence."
qwen3:4b is one example of a small model that Ollama lists with tool support. Model names change quickly, so check the “tools” badge on the model’s page at ollama.com/library. The docs make no promise that a model fits your RAM (ordinary memory), so test it: ollama ps shows what loaded while it runs.

title: Adopt the Pet
text:
2. Give it room to think
Ollama’s docs say the default context (the context length, which is the same thing as the context window: how much text the model can see at once) is 4k tokens on machines with under 24 GiB of video memory (VRAM, the memory on the graphics card or shared with it), which includes a 16 GB laptop. Agents and coding tools need at least 64k, and OpenCode says it requires 64k or higher. Set it when you start the server:
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=64000 ollama serve
Check what loaded with ollama ps. A bigger context needs more memory and can push work onto the CPU (the main processor; graphics hardware is faster), which is slow, so the Pet may be a patient companion.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
Prerequisites: Recruit the Beast. Adopt the Pet is advised, not required. Objective: set the model and the effort on purpose, especially when you hand work to a subagent, and learn to compare two settings on your own task. Time: about 15 minutes. The exercise is a worksheet and needs no model.
Last verified (docs, not run): research/model-and-effort.md sources on 2026-11-17; the model-config, effort, sub-agents, costs, choosing-a-model and optimizing-for-cost pages were spot-checked live that day; model names, aliases and defaults change often
The companions in the Kennel are models; the tool around them (the harness, the program that runs the model and its tools) is the armour. This page is about which companion to bring to which job, and how hard to make it think. Model names, aliases and defaults change often, so check the current docs and your own tool before relying on any name here.
A few words first. A model tier is a size class of model: a smaller one is faster and cheaper, a larger one is more capable and costs more. An alias is a short nickname (such as sonnet) that the tool maps to a concrete model version. Effort is how much the model thinks before each step. A subagent is a helper the main agent starts with its own fresh context, which does a side task and returns only a summary. To delegate is to hand a task to a subagent. A token is a chunk of text, the unit that usage and cost are counted in, and context is the text the model can see right now. Frontmatter is the small settings block at the top of a Markdown file. To pin a model is to name one exact version so it never silently changes, and inherit means “use whatever the parent is using”. The prompt cache is a short-term store that makes re-reading an unchanged conversation cheaper.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
1. Two dials

Model is what the companion knows and can do.
Effort is how much it thinks per step. Lower effort means fewer and terser tool calls (the actions the agent takes, such as reading a file or running a command); higher effort means more thoroughness.

The docs say tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models. One article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs: effort cannot add knowledge the model lacks, so a model that does not know an unusual method will not find it by thinking longer. Treat that as a hypothesis to test.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
2. How to set them

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Model. Aliases the docs list: default (clears an override and names no model), best (same as opus), fable, sonnet, opus, haiku, sonnet[1m], opus[1m] (the [1m] forms ask for a longer context window), and opusplan (the opus model in plan mode, then sonnet for the execution). Plan mode is a mode in which the agent proposes a plan and edits nothing until you approve it. On the Anthropic API the docs map opus, sonnet and haiku to the current 5.5 versions; other providers can resolve the same alias to older versions.








Way
How
Note




In a session
/model <alias or name>
alone, it opens a picker; Enter saves it as your default, s keeps it for this session only


Per launch
claude --model <alias or name>



Environment
ANTHROPIC_MODEL



Settings file
model field




For results that must be reproducible (a lab pipeline, course material), pin a full model name such as claude-opus-5-5, because an alias moves when a new version ships (our inference from how aliases work). The docs also offer ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL and ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL to pin what each alias means.
Effort. /effort, claude --effort, the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, or the effortLevel setting. The levels are low, medium, high, xhigh and max, and which ones exist depends on the model. The default differs by model and by surface. For Sonnet 5.5, the Claude Code model-config page says medium, while the API effort page says high on the API, so name the surface before quoting a default, and run /effort in your own tool to read yours.
Per skill and per subagent. Both skill files and subagent files take model and effort in their frontmatter.

A skill’s model takes the same values as /model, or inherit. A skill’s model and effort apply for the rest of that one turn and are not saved. A skill’s effort overrides the session level but not CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL.
A subagent’s model takes sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, a full model ID, or inherit. Its effort takes low to max. If the subagent’s model differs from the main one and you give no effort, the session level does not apply to it, so set it.
Which model a subagent gets, first match wins: the per-call model parameter, then the definition’s model, then the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL, then the main conversation’s model.

A subagent is a Markdown file with frontmatter in .claude/agents/ (project) or ~/.claude/agents/ (yours). Sketch, not run:
---
name: log-reader
description: Reads long pipeline logs and reports only failed tasks with their error lines.
model: haiku
effort: medium
---
Read the logs you are given. Return: task name, exit status, the first error line.
Quote lines exactly. If something is unclear, say so.
A subagent definition can also limit what the helper may use (a tools field): the sub-agents docs in Lore below give the exact syntax, which this sketch leaves out.
Why medium? The docs say Haiku 5.5 at low is more likely to skip a search, stop early or skip a check, a poor trade for reading logs, where catching every failure is the point.



/models picks a model for the current session only; the config file is unchanged.
opencode run --model provider/model-id sets it for one run. The format is provider/model-id, with an optional #variant such as #high. IDs are case-sensitive.
The model key in opencode.json (or opencode.jsonc) sets your default.
An agent can have its own model key. A subagent with no model inherits the parent session’s model. The docs’ frontmatter example is mode: subagent plus model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5#high (sketch, not run).
A local Ollama model is selectable like any other, for example ollama/gemma3:4b, as the Adopt the Pet quest showed.

Not checked: which model OpenCode’s built-in general and explore subagents use, whether a small_model key exists, the file location for OpenCode agent files, and whether a local model is good enough as a cheap delegate (the docs only say it can be selected). Not checked: any way to run an Ollama model as a Claude Code subagent; Claude Code’s documented subagent model values are Claude aliases or Claude IDs only.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
3. A decision ladder
Where the docs speak, I say so: the docs list the smallest tier (Haiku) as suited to subagent tasks and say most workloads start with Opus. Everything else is General practice: a starting point to test on your own jobs. The docs name four tiers in this order of capability: Haiku (fastest replies and lowest cost), Sonnet (everyday coding and agent work), Opus (complex agentic coding), Fable (hardest, long-running work). Check the current docs; models change.









Job
Start with
Effort
Why (General practice unless noted)




Most everyday work, no better information
Opus (per the docs)
the tool’s default
the docs say most workloads start here


Bulk reading, classifying or extracting with output you can check
Haiku, often as a subagent
medium, or low if you re-run failures
cheap per item; a checker catches errors


Exploratory reading (“where is X handled?”)
a subagent
low or medium
the main context stays clean; only a summary returns


Planning a change (see Plan Before You Edit)
consider Opus or Fable
medium to high
a bad plan makes every later step wrong


Mechanical edits with tests that fail loudly
Sonnet
medium
the tests do the judging


Hardest multi-file change, or unfamiliar science
Opus or Fable
high, then up only if a check says it helps
per one article, effort cannot add knowledge the model lacks, so the model matters too

title: Pick Your Companion
section: 4. When the output is not good enough: the upgrade ladder
text:
4. When the output is not good enough: the upgrade ladder
Climb one rung at a time and re-check after each.

Add a way to verify. A test, a script, a count against an independent tool, a second look that does not share the first one’s blind spot (the idea behind Ground Truth). Without it you cannot tell whether the next rungs helped.
Raise effort one level.
Change the model to the next tier up.

The order (check, then effort, then model) is one article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs, though the docs do say to give the agent something to verify against and that effort is often the better lever. The article is a claude.dev piece about choosing a Claude model (the page shows the byline Addy Osmani and the date 2026-11-09, but does not say who runs the site, so authorship is unverified; its numbers are not verified). I use only its ideas, in my own words.
The cheap-then-retry pattern is in Anthropic’s cost-and-intelligence guidance for the API (a docs page, “Optimizing for cost and intelligence”): if outcomes are checkable (tests, or a verifier, which is a separate check that tests the output), run at low effort and re-run only the failures at higher effort. Two caveats from the same page: a checker that passes bad work lets failures through, and a failure costs two runs of waiting time. The docs also say to compare cost per finished task, because failed tasks still cost money and a few hard tasks can carry much of the bill.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
5. Delegation hygiene

Keep the expensive model’s context lean. Sending bulk reading to a subagent keeps that reading out of the main conversation (documented benefit).
A subagent returns only a summary, and summaries omit and distort. Spot-check: ask for exact quotes or file paths and open two yourself (see Where Machines Fail). Many subagents returning long answers can also fill the main context again, per the docs.
State your rules in the delegation prompt. Per the docs, the built-in Explore and Plan subagents (Explore is a read-only search helper; Plan is a read-only research helper used in plan mode) skip CLAUDE.md (the instructions file the tool loads at session start; see Know Your Gear) for speed, so a rule like “never touch raw/” must be written into the task you hand them. Custom subagents load it unless set to skip it.
Keep edits on the main model. One article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs: let a cheaper subagent read and report, and make the changes on the model you trust most.
Switching model mid-conversation can change prompt-cache behaviour (the docs say so and may ask you to confirm). One article’s advice, not confirmed in the docs: compact first, or switch at a natural break; compacting means replacing the history with a short summary (see When to Start Fresh).
Change effort between sessions when you are comparing. The docs note that changing top-level effort mid-session also invalidates the cache.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
6. Measure on your own task
Pick one small real task that has an outcome check (a test that passes, a count that matches).

Choose two settings to compare, for example the same model at medium and high. Change only one thing.
For each, start a fresh session, run the task three times, and record pass or fail from the outcome check.
After each run, open /usage and note the “Usage by model” block. The dollar figure is an estimate computed locally at list price, and on a subscription you may see plan usage bars instead. /usage resets on /clear.
Compare cost per passing run. Three runs is a small sample: it can expose a big difference, and a small one needs more runs.

This is the same habit as the Forest quests Close the Loop (give the agent something to check against) and Test the Skill (compare behaviour with and without a change).

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
7. What you gave up
Choosing wrongly costs you in both directions. Too small or too low: the companion loses the thread, skips checks or stops early, and you redo the work, often after you have already trusted it. Too big or too high: the same job costs more and runs slower, and you may not notice because the answer looks fine. The checks above are how you notice either mistake.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
Exercise: assign six jobs
No model needed. For each mock job, write down a model (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus or Fable), an effort (low, medium, high) and whether you would use a subagent, then open the key.

Rename 200 sample IDs in a samplesheet to a new scheme, given a mapping table.
Summarise the methods section of one paper into five bullets for your lab notes.
Debug a Nextflow stage that fails on one sample and passes on the others.
Classify 5,000 free-text tissue labels into 12 categories, with 200 hand-labelled rows to check against.
Plan a refactor of a 600-line QC script that three other people depend on.
Explain an error message you have not seen before.



Answer key (General practice, not from the docs; several answers are defensible)


Probably no model at all. A mapping table and a script do this exactly, and a script cannot invent an ID. If you use a model, Haiku at low or medium, with a diff or count check; no subagent needed.
Sonnet, medium, no subagent. The text is short, so there is no context to protect. Check two claims against the paper yourself.
Sonnet at medium, raised to high or Opus if the first attempt fails and a test says so. Keep it in the main conversation, because the debugging needs the history. Add a failing test first (rung 1).
Haiku, a subagent or a batch script, medium. The 200 hand-labelled rows are your outcome check; re-run only the rows that disagree at a higher setting. Spot-check a sample of the rest.
Opus, high, in plan mode, main conversation. A weak plan is expensive downstream and other people depend on the script. Ask for a test plan too (see Plan Before You Edit).
Sonnet, low or medium, no subagent. It is a short, checkable question: try the suggested fix. Escalate when the explanation does not hold up.



Check what model and effort your tool is using right now (/model, /effort) and write them down.


Run the same small task at two settings and compare the result and /usage.

title: Ground Truth
text:
Prerequisites: Spot the Mirage, a terminal with Python 3 and awk, and the two exercise files below (about 1 KB in total). Nothing here touches your own data. Objective: find out whether a script an agent called “tested” is actually right, using a check the agent did not write. Time: about 15 minutes.
Verified: ran gc.py and the awk check on 2026-11-13 (macOS, Python 3.15, Apple awk). Output below is the real output.
Files: tiny.fasta and gc.py. Save both into an empty folder.

title: Ground Truth
text:
The lantern
An agent gave you gc.py, which reports the GC content of each sequence, and said “tested, works”. Test it yourself:
python gc.py tiny.fasta
You should see:
seq1    50.0
seq2    20.0
seq3    25.0
Now measure the same thing a different way, with a tool the agent did not write. This awk command uppercases each line, counts G and C, and counts the total length:
awk '/^>/{if(n)print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"; n=substr($1,2); gc=0; t=0; next}
     {s=toupper($0); t+=length(s); gc+=gsub(/[GC]/,"",s)}
     END{print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"}' tiny.fasta
seq1    6 GC of 12 total
seq2    6 GC of 10 total
seq3    2 GC of 8 total
Work out the percentages and compare them row by row with the script. Two of the three rows tell a story, and one of them is not a bug at all. Then take the battle.

title: Ground Truth
text: Battle: the lantern

title: Ground Truth
text:
Lore
Further reading. Optional.

title: Boss: The Wall of Output
text:
Prerequisites: Ground Truth. This is the boss at the end of the trunk. Objective: survive a wall of agent output without reading all of it and without trusting all of it. Time: about 10 minutes. Each right answer on the first try damages the boss.
Practice guidance, not a vendor claim. Based on the habits taught in this zone.

title: Boss: The Wall of Output
text:
The Wall
The Wall is thousands of lines of generated diff (the list of lines a change added and removed), produced faster than anyone can review. If you merge it unread, the Blight spreads. If you try to read all of it, your attention thins and you approve things you did not understand. Both routes fail.
The way through is to refuse it whole: keep a review budget (only produce as much as you can honestly review today, because bulk low-quality output is called slop), ask for smaller pieces, ground each piece in a check, and pass on only work you have read yourself.

title: Send Small, Say So
text:
Prerequisites: Spot the Mirage. The Wall of Output is advised. Objective: hand work to collaborators, whether or not they use LLMs, without passing them your review burden. Time: about 15 minutes. General practice, not a vendor claim. Not checked: any venue’s disclosure policy. Team norms you agree locally override these defaults.
A reef is a community. When you use an agent, the cost of checking its output must not silently land on the next person. The Review-leech feeds on exactly that.
Four habits:
These help reviewers who use LLMs and those who do not. A colleague who does not use LLMs can review your work without learning a tool.

title: Send Small, Say So
section: When you worry about looking lazy
text:
When you worry about looking lazy
A common worry: people will think I am lazy or unoriginal for using it. You can make the facts easy to see.

Say plainly what the agent did and what you checked. “The agent drafted the plotting code. I read it and compared the output with a hand calculation.”
Follow your team’s norm. Some groups want a note in the commit message, some in the methods. Use what yours agrees on.
Let the evidence speak. Tests, checks and your ability to explain every line show the work is yours.
Ask. A lead or a journal editor can tell you what they expect.
Check the venue. Some venues have disclosure policies. If you name one, read its own page and cite it.

Prerequisites: Send Small, Say So. Objective: review work that involved an LLM, kindly and effectively, and choose formats that review well. Time: about 15 minutes. General practice, not a vendor claim. Team norms you agree locally override these defaults.
You will also be on the receiving end. Reviewing LLM-assisted work is the same craft as any review, with a few shifts in attention.

title: The Reviewer’s Code
text:
Formats that review well
Notebooks are one example. A marimo notebook is stored as a plain .py file, so a diff shows what changed. A Jupyter .ipynb is JSON that also stores outputs and run counts, so diffs are noisy and hard to read, though stripping tools exist. If you ask an agent to produce analysis, prefer a format your reviewer can actually diff.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
Prerequisites: Save Point (for git diff). Jupyter experience helps but is not required. Objective: explain why a one-line change to a notebook produces a noisy diff, and name four ways to make the change reviewable. Time: about 15 minutes.
Verified: ran diff and git diff --no-index --stat on the mock notebooks on 2026-11-16 (macOS, Python 3.9.6). Tool facts: Last verified (docs, not run): nbformat, nbstripout, jupytext, nbdime and marimo docs on 2026-11-16.
Files: before.ipynb and after.ipynb, two tiny mock notebooks (about 2.5 KB each). They are mock files: they omit cell ids, so they are not strictly valid nbformat 4.5. Save both into an empty folder.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
section: A notebook is a JSON file
text:
A notebook is a JSON file
A .ipynb file is a JSON document with metadata, nbformat, nbformat_minor (the notebook file-format version numbers) and a list of cells. A code cell stores its source, but also an execution_count and its outputs. A plot is stored inside the file as a base64 string (the image bytes written out as plain text). The format keeps source and outputs in the same file, so any run rewrites lines next to the code.
Whether you use an agent or not, this is what git sees. The two mock notebooks differ by one real change: the cutoff 30 became 40. Compare them:
diff before.ipynb after.ipynb
5c5
<    "execution_count": 3,
---
>    "execution_count": 7,
8c8
<     "print(len([r for r in reads if r >= 30]))"
---
>     "print(len([r for r in reads if r >= 40]))"
15c15
<       "3\n"
---
>       "2\n"
21c21
<       "image/png": "AAECAwQFBgcICQoLDA0ODxAREhMUFRYXGBkaGx...
---
>       "image/png": "AAMGCQwPEhUYGx4hJCcqLTAzNjk8P0JFSEtOUV...
Four changed spots, one of them is the code. The rest is the run counter, the printed result and an image blob. General practice, not measured here: in a real notebook an image is often tens of kilobytes on a single line, and there are usually many cells. The format docs describe the structure; that this makes diffs noisy is our reading of it, and the output above is the evidence.
The risk with a coding agent is the same as with a human: a reviewer who cannot find the code change will approve without reading it.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
section: Four ways to make changes reviewable
text:
Four ways to make changes reviewable
Each of these is one option among several. Each moves the noise somewhere else.








Option
What it does
Cost




nbstripout
Strips outputs and some metadata when git stores the notebook. Outputs stay in your working file, so on its own it does not change what an agent reads.
Git cannot set up the filter on clone, so each collaborator runs nbstripout --install themselves.


jupytext
Pairs the .ipynb with a .py (the py:percent format is recommended for code). You review the .py; outputs stay in the .ipynb.
Two files to keep in sync.


nbdime
A notebook-aware diff: nbdiff in the terminal, nbdiff-web in the browser, with git integration and a merge driver.
Everyone reviewing needs it installed.


marimo
Notebooks are stored as pure Python, so ordinary git diffs work.
A different notebook tool from Jupyter. marimo convert your_notebook.ipynb > your_notebook.py converts an existing one.



General practice: the costs above are our judgement, except the nbstripout clone limit, which is from its docs. Pick by what your team can adopt; stripping outputs is likely the smallest change and a different notebook tool the largest.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
Review the code cells
Whatever you choose, the review habit is the same:

Look at the source cells. Treat outputs as something to regenerate.
Run git diff --stat before committing and look for a notebook that grew by megabytes.
An output in a diff shows that something ran once; a re-run shows whether the code produces it.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
With a companion

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Claude Code reads a .ipynb with all its cells and outputs, and an output-heavy notebook fills context. It edits notebooks with NotebookEdit, one cell at a time, by cell_id. Replacing a code cell clears that cell’s execution count and saved outputs, so the agent’s diff in the notebook contains lost outputs as well as new source. Note that nbstripout is a git filter: outputs stay in the working file, so on its own it does not change what the agent’s Read returns. To keep the agent on the code, strip outputs from the working copy (nbstripout’s pre-commit mode modifies the working copy, per its docs) or point the agent at the paired .py. That is general practice; check the docs for your version.


The idea is the same: review the source cells. This quest has no tool-specific claims for OpenCode; check its docs for how it handles notebook files.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
Honour

Run git diff –stat in one of your own repositories that contains a notebook, and note how much of the change is outputs.


Write one sentence naming which of the four options your team could adopt this week, and what each collaborator would have to do.

title: Plan: accept a new strandedness column in the samplesheet
text:
Plan: accept a new strandedness column in the samplesheet
Task given to the agent: “Our samplesheet gets a new optional column, strandedness (values: forward, reverse, unstranded). Make parse_samplesheet.py accept it.”

Read bin/parse_samplesheet.py and tests/test_parse_samplesheet.py to see how columns are read.
Add strandedness to the list of known columns in parse_samplesheet.py, defaulting to unstranded when the column is absent.
Build the parsed result as a dictionary keyed by sample_id, since sample IDs are unique, so downstream code can look a sample up directly.
Rename the parameter --input_sheet to --samplesheet in conf/base.config so it matches the new parser option name.
Update the alignment and counting modules, the documentation and the test suite so the whole pipeline uses strandedness end to end.
Tell the user the parser now handles the new column.

text:
